game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Four dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 3, 3, 5, 5, 10, 11.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 12.
- Die 4 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 3, 5, 9, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Expected sum is about 18.58 (the four dice average 3.667, 4.875, 5.375 and 4.667), with a standard deviation of about 6.9. The share of informed traders is unknown and averages about 0.48, so I'm quoting a wide spread centred on 18.6.

{"bid": 14.1, "ask": 23.1}

A counterparty sold to me at 14.1, which is well below the prior mean. That is mild evidence the true sum is low, so I lower my fair value and skew my quotes down a little to shed some of my long position.

**Prior for the sum**
- Expected value of each die: 3.67 + 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.67 ≈ 18.6.
- Standard deviation of the sum: about 6.9.

**Effect of the sale at 14.1**
- The chance the true value is below 14.1 is roughly 0.27.
- The chance a noise trader values it below 14.1 is roughly 0.22.
- So the sale only slightly favours an informed seller. If the seller was informed, the value is likely around 10.
- Averaging over the possible values of alpha, my fair value moves to about 17.5.

**Quote**
- I am long 1 unit, so I shade both prices down a little.
- I keep the spread wide because I don't know alpha yet.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 21.5}

The posterior estimate of the settlement value is about 13, and I'm quoting around it.

**Prior value given die 1 = 1:**
- Die 2 has mean 4.875.
- Die 3 has mean 5.375.
- Die 4 has mean about 4.67.
- The expected sum is about 15.9, with a standard deviation of about 6.5 from the three unrevealed dice.

**What the trades suggest:**
- The counterparty at quote 3 sold to me at 12.3 after die 1 was revealed. If they were informed, the value is below 12.3. That outcome has a prior probability of roughly 29%.
- The sale at 14.1 in stage 1 also points to a low value.
- I don't know the share of informed counterparties, so I shade my estimate down to about 13.

**Quote:**
- I'm long 2 and this is the last quote of the round, so I'm happy to sell.
- I'll put the ask a bit above fair value, so a noise trader may well buy from me.
- I'll keep the bid well below fair value to guard against informed sellers.

{"bid": 10.4, "ask": 15.4}

Prior fair value is the sum of the four dice means: 3.667 + 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.667 ≈ 18.58. The standard deviation of the sum is about 6.9.

**What Round 1 says about alpha:**
- At quote 2 (bid 13.5) there was no trade. An informed trader valuing at 11 would have sold, so that counterparty was a noise trader.
- At quote 4 the counterparty sold at 10.4. An informed trader valuing at 11 would not have sold there, so that was also a noise trader.
- Two confirmed noise traders in four quotes make alpha = 0.9 unlikely. My rough posterior is about 0.41 on alpha = 0.05, 0.54 on 0.5 and 0.05 on 0.9. That gives an expected alpha of about 0.35.

**Choosing the spread:** I traded off the spread earned from noise traders against expected losses to informed traders on each side. With alpha around 0.35, that is maximised at a half-spread of about 6 to 7 around 18.6.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 24.7}

The expected sum is about 18.6 (die means 3.67 + 4.88 + 5.38 + 4.67), with a standard deviation of about 6.9.

**Round 1 evidence on alpha:**
- At quote 2 (bid 13.5) there was no trade, but an informed counterparty would have sold, since the value was 11.
- At quote 4 the counterparty sold at 10.4, below the value of 11. Only a noise trader would do that.
- So alpha = 0.9 is unlikely, and alpha is probably 0.05 or 0.5.

**This round:** the wide quote 12.5 / 24.7 drew no trade, which hints slightly that the value is in the middle. I'll quote fairly wide around 18.6 to earn from noise traders while limiting losses to possibly informed ones.

{"bid": 14.5, "ask": 22.8}

Public fair value is about 16.2. Die 1 = 4, and the three unrevealed dice have a combined mean of about 14.9, which would give 18.9. I pull that down because the stage-1 sell at 14.5 was partly informed flow, and an informed seller implies a low total.

I estimate alpha at roughly 0.33. In round 1 there were three hits on my bid and the settlement was 11, which points to informed traders. But the 10.4 sell is inconsistent with an informed counterparty, since 11 was above my bid. That rules out alpha = 0.9 for practical purposes.

The remaining dice have a standard deviation of about 6.5 and adverse selection is moderate, so I use a half-spread of about 3.5–4. I skew slightly lower because I'm long one unit.

{"bid": 12.4, "ask": 19.6}

Die 1 is 4. The other three dice have mean 14.92 and SD about 6.5, so the prior expected value is about 18.9.

**Who I'm trading against (alpha).** Round 1 mostly points to noise traders:
- At quote 2, an informed trader would have sold at 13.5 because the value was 11. Nobody traded.
- At quote 4, someone sold at 10.4. An informed trader wouldn't do that with the value at 11.

My posterior is roughly 0.41 on alpha = 0.05, 0.55 on alpha = 0.5 and 0.05 on alpha = 0.9.

**Where the value sits.** This round counterparties sold to me at 14.5 and at 12.4. A noise trader would sell at 12.4 only about 13% of the time, so these sales push the estimate down. I put about 45% on the value being below 12.4 (mean about 9.5 there) and the rest around 20. That gives a fair value of roughly 14.5–15.

**The quote.** I'm long 2 and this is the last quote of the round, so I lean toward selling. I'll quote a wide bid below fair and an ask slightly above it.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 16.4}

No information has been revealed yet this round, so I quote around the prior mean of the dice sum.

**Expected value and spread of the sum**
- Die 1 has mean 22/6 ≈ 3.67.
- Die 2 has mean 39/8 = 4.875.
- Die 3 has mean 43/8 = 5.375.
- Die 4 has mean 28/6 ≈ 4.67.
- The sum has mean ≈ 18.58 and standard deviation ≈ 6.9.

**What the history says about alpha**
- At least 5 of the 8 counterparties so far acted in ways an informed trader would not:
  - Round 1: no one sold at 13.5 with value 11.
  - Round 1: someone sold at 10.4 with value 11.
  - Round 2: someone sold at 14.5 and at 12.4 with value 22.
- If alpha were 0.9, that many noise traders would be very unlikely, so it is almost ruled out.
- Alpha is most likely 0.05 or 0.5.
- That supports a moderately wide spread, slightly tighter than before, centred on 18.6.

{"bid": 14.4, "ask": 22.8}

Fair value is about 20.4, and I'm quoting a bid of 16.0 and an ask of 24.4, roughly ±4 around it.

**Prior expected sum.** The die means are 3.67, 4.88, 5.38 and 4.67, so the sum's expected value is about 18.6 with a standard deviation of about 6.9.

**How informed the counterparties look (alpha).** I compared each past trade with how the round actually settled.
- Four trades went against the settlement value, so they were noise traders: the round 1 no-trade at 13.5, the round 1 sale at 10.4, and the round 2 sales at 14.5 and 12.4.
- That makes alpha = 0.9 very unlikely.
- Weighing every trade and no-trade so far, the posterior is roughly 65% on alpha = 0.05 and 35% on alpha = 0.5. That gives an expected alpha of about 0.2.

**What the buy at 22.8 tells me.** The chance this buyer was informed is about 22%. If they were, the value is above 22.8, which averages about 27. Weighting that against the prior of 18.6 puts the fair value at about 20.4.

**Quote.** Being short 1 unit is only a slight reason to lean higher, so I'm leaving the quote close to centred on fair value.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 24.4}

I value the contract at about 17. With die 1 revealed as 1, the other three dice average about 14.9, so the base fair value is about 15.9. The buy at 22.8 earlier this round adds some chance that an informed trader knew the sum was high. That pushes my estimate up to roughly 17.

On how many counterparties are informed, several earlier trades could only have come from noise traders. For example, someone sold at 10.4 in round 1 when the contract settled at 11, so a trader who knew the value would not have sold. That suggests the informed share is low to moderate, probably 5% or 50% rather than 90%.

So I quote a moderately wide market around 17. I am short 1 unit, which is comfortable within the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 20.6}

Die 1 is 1. The expected sum of the other three dice is 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.667 ≈ 14.92, so the base fair value is about 15.9, with a standard deviation of about 6.5.

The trades so far this round are mixed evidence:
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at 22.8. That leans the value higher, but it's hard to square with die 1 = 1.
- **Quote 3:** nobody traded at 13.4 / 20.6. If that counterparty was informed, the value lies between those prices.

Both can't come from informed traders, so at least one was noise. I put fair value at about 16.5 and keep a wide spread, because alpha may be high.

{"bid": 13.2, "ask": 20.2}

Fair value is about 18.8, and I'm quoting bid 14.6 / ask 23.2.

**Prior expected value.** The die means are 3.67 + 4.88 + 5.38 + 4.67, which gives about 18.6. The standard deviation of the sum is about 6.9.

**How informed the counterparties are.** Six of the 13 past outcomes could not have come from an informed trader. Examples are selling at 10.4 when settlement was 11, and buying at 22.8 when settlement was 18. That makes alpha = 0.9 very unlikely. Most of the probability goes to alpha = 0.05, with some left on 0.5.

**Current fair value.** The buy at 22.6 this round shifts fair value up only slightly, to about 18.8.

**Spread.** Against noise traders with standard deviation 5.9, the profit-maximising distance from fair value is about 0.75 × 5.9 ≈ 4.4 on each side. I widen that a little for the remaining chance of informed traders. I also shade both quotes slightly upward because I'm short 1.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 23.2}

With die 1 revealed as 5, fair value is about 19.9 and I'm quoting 15.5 / 24.3, roughly 4.4 either side.

**Fair value.** The expected values of the unrevealed dice are:
- Die 2: 39/8 = 4.875
- Die 3: 43/8 = 5.375
- Die 4: 28/6 ≈ 4.67

Adding die 1 gives a fair value of about 19.9. The standard deviation of the remaining dice is about 6.5.

**Share of informed traders.** At least five past trades could not have come from someone who knew the settlement value:
- Round 1, quote 4: they sold at 10.4 when it settled at 11.
- Round 2, quotes 1 and 2: they sold at 14.5 and 12.4 when it settled at 22.
- Round 3, quote 1: they bought at 22.8 when it settled at 18.
- Round 3, quote 4: they sold at 13.2 when it settled at 18.

This makes the 0.9 case very unlikely, and the 0.05 case is favoured over 0.5. Mostly I'm facing noise traders.

**Spread.** Against noise traders with standard deviation 5.9, profit per quote is highest at a half-spread of about 0.75 × 5.9 ≈ 4.4. A small allowance for informed traders keeps it slightly wide. With position 0, there is no need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 24.3}

Fair value with die 1 = 5 is about 19.9: the three unrevealed dice average 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.667 ≈ 14.9. Their combined standard deviation is about 6.5.

The settlements so far suggest alpha is moderate, probably 0.5 or 0.05. The trades look like a mix of informed and noise counterparties.

Last quote (15.5 / 24.3) got no trade. That hints the value lies inside that range, so I can quote a bit tighter around about 19.9. I'm flat with one quote left in the round.

{"bid": 16.2, "ask": 23.6}

The contract's prior expected value is about 18.6, with a standard deviation of about 6.9. I'm quoting roughly ±4 around that.

**Expected value of each die:**
- Die 1: 22/6 ≈ 3.67
- Die 2: 39/8 ≈ 4.88
- Die 3: 43/8 ≈ 5.38
- Die 4: 28/6 ≈ 4.67

**How informed the counterparties seem:** Many past trades went against the settlement value, which means those counterparties could not have been informed:
- Round 2: they sold at 14.5 and 12.4, but it settled at 22.
- Round 3: they bought at 22.8 and sold at 13.2, but it settled at 18.
- Round 4: they bought at 22.6 and sold at 14.6, but it settled at 22.

So alpha is most likely 0.05 or 0.5, not 0.9. That supports a moderately tight spread around fair value.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 22.6}

The posterior points strongly to a low informed share (alpha around 0.05), so I'm quoting mainly for noise traders around a fair value of about 18.8.

- **Prior fair value:** the four dice have means 3.667, 4.875, 5.375 and 4.667, so the expected sum is 18.58.

  - Most past fills were on the wrong side of the settlement value, so they came from noise traders. Examples:

  - Very few trades look like informed trades.
- **This round's buy:** the buy at 22.6 says little under a low alpha. I nudge fair value up slightly to about 18.8.
- **Spread:** against noise with standard deviation 5.9, profit per quote is highest with a half-spread of about 0.75 × 5.9 ≈ 4.4.
- **Skew:** I'm short 1, so I lean the quote slightly upward.

{"bid": 14.5, "ask": 23.2}

The public fair value is about 19.5, so I'll quote 16.4 bid / 23.4 ask, roughly ±3.5 around it.

**Fair value before this round's trades.** With die 1 revealed as 3, the expected sum is 3 + 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.667 ≈ 17.9. The standard deviation of the three hidden dice is about 6.5.

**How informed the counterparties seem.** Several past trades went the wrong way for an informed trader. In round 3 someone bought at 22.8 and it settled at 18. In round 4 someone sold at 14.6 and it settled at 22. So the informed share is probably 0.05 or 0.5, not 0.9.

**This round's trades.** Both counterparties bought, at 22.6 and 23.2. That is a mild sign the sum is high, which pushes fair value up to about 19.5.

**Position.** I'm short 2, so I keep the quotes roughly centred but don't lower them. That keeps the bid fairly competitive for buying back.

{"bid": 16.4, "ask": 23.4}

Die 1 = 3, so the prior expected settlement is 3 + 4.875 + 5.375 + 4.667 ≈ 17.9, with a standard deviation of about 6.5.

**What the trades say.** Two counterparties bought at asks of 22.6 and 23.2, well above the fair value at the time (about 18.6). Then quote 3 at 16.4 / 23.4 got no trade.

**How informed are they?** Earlier rounds show both informed-looking and noise-looking trades, so I treat alpha as moderate.

**Revised value.** With moderate alpha, the two buys strongly point to a high value. My rough posterior puts most of the weight on a settlement of 24 or more. Blending across the possible alphas gives an expected value of about 22–23, with the upside skewed.

**Quote.** I'm short 2 and this is the last quote of the round. I want to buy back if offered, and I don't want to sell cheaply to an informed buyer. So I keep a low-to-mid bid and a high ask.

{"bid": 20.5, "ask": 27.0}

The expected settlement value is 18.6, so I quote about ±4.3 around it: bid 14.3, ask 22.9.

**Fair value.** Each die's average:
- Die 1: 22/6 = 3.67
- Die 2: 39/8 = 4.875

- Die 4: 28/6 = 4.67

These sum to 18.58.

**Spread.** Against noise traders with standard deviation 5.9, the best half-spread is about 0.75 × 5.9 ≈ 4.4. That gives the quote below.

{"bid": 14.3, "ask": 22.9}

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 23.4}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 7, 9, 11, 11, 12.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 4, 11.
- Die 3 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 4, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The expected settlement is the sum of the three die means:

- Die 1: (2+7+9+11+11+12)/6 ≈ 8.67
- Die 2: (1+3+4+11)/4 = 4.75
- Die 3: (0+0+4+6)/4 = 2.5

Fair value is about 15.92, with a standard deviation of about 5.7.

The informed share (alpha) is unknown and averages about 0.48. That makes informed traders a real risk, so I quote about ±3.5 around fair value. Noise traders, whose noise has a standard deviation of 4.8, will still trade at that width some of the time.

{"bid": 12.4, "ask": 19.4}

Fair value now looks like about 19.6, so I'm quoting a wide market around it.

**Before any trades:** the expected sum is 8.67 + 4.75 + 2.5 = 15.92.

**What the buy at 19.4 tells me:**
- An informed trader buys only if the sum is 20 or more. That happens with probability about 0.26. In that case the expected sum is about 23.2.
- A noise trader buys with about the same probability, roughly 0.23, so the trade says almost nothing about alpha.
- Weighting the three possible alphas by how likely each makes this buy, the buyer was informed with probability about 0.5.
- That puts the updated fair value at about 15.92 + 0.5 × 7.2 ≈ 19.6.

**Why the quote is wide:** alpha could be as high as 0.9, the sum's distribution is skewed and lumpy, and fair value itself is still uncertain. I keep a wide quote around 19.6 and lean slightly toward buying back, since I'm currently short 1.

{"bid": 15.4, "ask": 24.2}

Die 2 = 1, so the settlement S = die 1 + die 3 + 1, with a prior mean of about 12.17.

**What the trades tell me**
- **Quote 1 (buy at 19.4):** with die 2 = 1 the maximum possible settlement is 12 + 6 + 1 = 19. An informed trader would not have bought at 19.4, so that buyer was a noise trader. This makes a low alpha more likely.
- **Quote 2 (no trade at 15.4 / 24.2):** an informed trader would have sold if S < 15.4. No trade therefore shifts weight towards the high outcomes, S of 16 to 19 (7 of the 24 outcomes).

**Updated estimates**
- Fair value: about 13.0.
- The chance S is one of the high outcomes is about 0.40.
- Alpha: 0.05 with probability about 0.67, 0.5 with about 0.28 and 0.9 with about 0.05. The expected alpha is about 0.22.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Ask:** I traded off noise-buyer profit against informed buys when S is 18 or 19. The expected profit is about flat between 16.5 and 17.5, and best at about 17.5 (around +0.57 per quote).
- **Bid:** most low outcomes are 3 to 9. Bids between 8.5 and 9.5 give nearly the same expected profit, about +0.54, so I picked 9.0.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 17.5}

The contract's expected value is now about 14.6, and I'm quoting wide around it: bid 11.5, ask 19.0.

**Value range.** Die 2 is 1, so the contract settles at 1 + die 1 + die 3. That puts it between 3 and 19, with a prior mean of about 12.17.

**What the earlier trades say about how many traders are informed.**
- In quote 1 someone bought at 19.4. With die 2 = 1 the contract can be worth at most 19, so an informed trader would never pay 19.4. That buyer was almost certainly a noise trader.
- This makes a low informed share likely. My estimate is about 0.57 that 5% of traders are informed, 0.33 that 50% are, and 0.10 that 90% are.

**What the trades say about the value.**
- In quote 3 someone bought at 17.5. An informed trader only does that if the value is 18 or 19.
- In quote 2 nobody sold at 15.4. An informed trader stays out there whenever the value is 16 or more, which fits the same picture.
- Together these raise the chance the value is 18 or 19 to about 44%. The chance it is 16 or 17 is about 14%, and the chance it is lower is about 43%.
- The expected value is about 14.6.

**This quote (last of the round, I'm short 2).**
- **Ask 19.0:** an informed trader can never profitably buy at 19.0, since the value is at most 19. A noise trader still buys about 18% of the time and pays roughly 4.4 above expected value.
- **Bid 11.5:** an informed trader sells only if the value is below 11.5. That case is unlikely and mostly comes with a low informed share. A noise trader sells about a quarter of the time, roughly 3 below expected value.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 19.0}

This round the dice have not been revealed, so fair value is the sum of the three dice means: 8.67 + 4.75 + 2.5 ≈ 15.92.

**Inferring alpha from round 1**
- **Quote 1:** a counterparty bought at 19.4, but settlement was 13. An informed trader would not have bought, so this was noise.
- **Quote 2:** no trade, with my bid at 15.4. An informed trader valuing at 13 would have sold, so this was probably noise.
- **Quote 3:** a counterparty bought at 17.5 when fair value was about 12.2. That was noise again.
- **Quote 4:** no trade. This fits either type.

The posterior is about 0.82 that alpha = 0.05, 0.18 that alpha = 0.5, and close to 0 that alpha = 0.9.

**Setting the spread**
- Against noise traders (standard deviation 4.8), the best distance from fair value is about 0.75 × 4.8 ≈ 3.6.
- Informed traders are now probably rare, but the settlement value is widely spread (standard deviation about 5.7), so I add a little extra width.
- That gives a bid of 12.0 and an ask of 19.8 around the fair value of 15.92.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 19.8}

Alpha is probably low, so I'll quote about 3.6 either side of the expected value of 15.9.

**Expected value.** Die 1 averages 8.67, die 2 averages 4.75 and die 3 averages 2.5, so the expected sum is about 15.92.

**Evidence on alpha (how often traders are informed).**
- Round 1 settled at 13.
- In round 1, buyers paid 19.4 and 17.5, both above the true value. An informed trader would not have bought at either price.
- At quote 2, my bid was 15.4. An informed trader valuing the contract at 13 would have sold to me there, and nobody did.
- Together these point strongly to alpha = 0.05, so most traders are noise traders.

**Quote.** Against noise traders with noise of standard deviation 4.8, profit per side is roughly the half-spread times the chance a trader crosses it. That is highest at about 0.75 standard deviations, or roughly 3.6. Centring on 15.9 gives a bid of 12.3 and an ask of 19.5.

- **Settlement spread is wide.** The total can land anywhere from 5 to 21. Informed traders would take advantage of a tight quote, so I keep a wide one.

With three dice, the expected settlement is 8.67 + 4.75 + 2.5 ≈ 15.9.

- **Round 2:** Settlement was 5, well below my bids. An informed counterparty would have sold to me at every quote. All 4 quotes went untraded.
  - If alpha = 0.5, that is roughly 0.7% likely.
  - If alpha = 0.05, it is roughly 8.5% likely.

Alpha is almost certainly about 0.05, so I'm quoting a wide, symmetric spread around fair value to earn from noise traders.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 6, 6, 7, 7, 12, 12, 12, 12.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 6, 7.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Before any reveal the expected sum is 13, but the outcome is lumpy, so I'll quote wide and keep only small exposure to informed traders.

**Settlement distribution**
- Die 1 is 6 (1/4), 7 (1/4) or 12 (1/2).
- Die 2 is 1 (1/2), 6 (1/4) or 7 (1/4).
- The sum is 7 or 8 with probability 1/8 each, and 12 or 14 with probability 1/16 each.
- It is 13 with probability 3/8, and 18 or 19 with probability 1/8 each.
- The mean is 13.

**Choosing the quote**
- Alpha is unknown and its prior average is about 0.48, so many counterparties may know the value exactly.
- A narrow quote such as 11/15 loses money against informed traders: they buy at 15 whenever the sum is 18 or 19.
- Quoting just inside the tails (7.5 and 18.5) limits the expected loss to informed traders to about 0.06 per side.
- Each side still earns roughly 0.26 per quote from noise traders.
- This quote also shows how counterparties trade, which helps me estimate alpha for later quotes.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 18.5}

The fair value is 13.0, and quoting wide at 7.6 / 18.4 has the best expected value.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 averages 9.25 and die 2 averages 3.75, so the sum averages 13.0.
- The possible sums and their chances are:
  - 7 and 8: 1/8 each
  - 12: 1/16
  - 13: 3/8
  - 14: 1/16
  - 18 and 19: 1/8 each
- Half the probability sits at the extremes (7–8 or 18–19). An informed trader therefore usually has a large edge against a tight quote.
- The no-trade at 7.5 / 18.5 slightly lowers the chance of a 7 or a 19, but fair value stays about 13.

**Choosing the half-spread (h)**
I weighed the edge from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders. The average alpha is about 0.48.

| Half-spread | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 3 | about −0.04 |
| 4 | about +0.11 |
| 5 | about +0.21 |
| 5.4 (quote 7.6 / 18.4) | about +0.26 |

At 7.6 / 18.4, only an informed trader who knows the value is 7 or 19 would trade, and loses me just 0.4 each time. That leaves noise traders with some chance to trade. Any trade also tells me something about alpha for later rounds.

**Ask side.**

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 2, 4 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 6, 4 cards worth 7, 4 cards worth 11, 4 cards worth 15. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The fair value of the two-card sum is about 13.8, and I'm quoting about 5 either side of it at 8.8 / 18.8.

**Fair value of the sum**
- The deck totals 152 across 22 cards, so one card averages about 6.91.
- Two cards therefore average about 13.82.
- One card has a variance of about 27.5.
- Drawing two cards without replacement gives a variance of about 52.4, a standard deviation of about 7.2.

**Spread**
- The share of informed traders is unknown and averages about 0.48 across the three possibilities, so it could be high.
- The sum varies a lot (standard deviation about 7.2), so a narrow quote would lose heavily to informed traders.
- Noise traders' valuations have a standard deviation of 6.2, so a quote about 5 either side of fair value still trades with them reasonably often.
- I'm quoting a symmetric spread of about ±5 around 13.8.

{"bid": 8.8, "ask": 18.8}

The quote-1 sale at 8.8 makes the fair value about 9, so I centre near 9 with a wide spread.

**Prior fair value.** The deck's 22 cards sum to 152, so the average card is 6.91. Two cards average 13.82, with a standard deviation of about 7.2.

**What the sale tells me.**
- An informed trader sells at 8.8 only if the true sum is 8 or less.
  - That happens in 57 of the 231 possible two-card hands, so 24.7% of the time.
  - When it does, the average sum is about 4.5.
- A noise trader sells at 8.8 about 21% of the time, and that tells me nothing about the cards.
- I don't know alpha, the chance that a trader is informed. The sale barely changes my view of it.
- Averaging over the three possible alpha values, the expected sum after this sale is about **9.0**.

**Quote.**
- The fair value is now about 9.
- Informed traders could be a large share of the flow, so I keep the spread wide.
- I'm already long 1, so I set the ask a little closer to the fair value than the bid to make a sale more likely.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 13.0}

Card 1 is a 3, so the total is 3 plus card 2. Weighing the 21 cards still in the deck by how well each fits the trading so far gives an expected settlement of about 6.9.

**How the trades shift the estimate**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 8.8. An informed trader would only sell there if the total were below 8.8, meaning card 2 is 0, 2 or 3.
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded at 4.5 / 13. An informed trader would have traded if the total were 3 (sell) or 14 or more (buy). So for an informed trader, only card 2 = 2 or 3 fits both quotes.
- **Effect:** these two outcomes make a high share of informed traders more likely. Combined, they shift the weight heavily towards a total of 5–6.

**Approximate weights on the total**

| Total | Card 2 | Share of weight |
|---|---|---|
| 5–6 | 2 or 3 | about 66% |
| 3 | 0 | about 13% |
| 9–10 | 6 or 7 | about 11% |
| 14–18 | 11 or 15 | about 10% |

**Quoting**
- **Bid 4.5:** below the likely range, so an informed seller only hits it when the total is 3, costing about 1.5. Noise traders, centred near 6.9, sell there fairly often and earn me about 2.4 each.
- **Ask 9.5:** I'm long 1, so I'm happy to sell. At 9.5, an informed buyer only takes it when the total is 10 or more. Noise traders buy above fair value often enough to pay for that risk.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 9.5}

Bid 3.0 and ask 10.0 for the last quote. My estimate of the settlement value is about 6.2, and the bid is set so an informed trader can't sell to me at a loss.

**Prior after the reveal.** Card 1 is 3, so 21 cards remain with a total value of 149. Their average is about 7.10, which puts the expected settlement near 10.1 before using the trades.

**What the trades say.** Counterparties sold to me at 8.8 and again at 4.5, and nobody traded on my 4.5 / 13 quote.
- If card 2 is 0, the settlement is 3. That fits both sales, but an informed trader would also have sold at 4.5 in quote 2.
- No single settlement value matches every quote being informed, so some of these trades came from noise traders.
- Weighting each possible settlement value by these trades, over the three possible alpha values, gives:
  - settlement 3 (card 2 = 0) is about 47% likely;
  - settlement 5 or 6 is about 29% likely;
  - settlement 14 or 18 is about 13% likely.

**This quote.**
- **Bid 3.0:** an informed seller would only sell if the settlement were below 3, which can't happen. So only noise traders hit this bid, at well under my 6.2 estimate.
- **Ask 10.0:** an informed buyer only takes it if the settlement is 14 or 18, about 13% likely. Noise buyers, judging from a higher public fair value, give a solid profit, and selling also trims my +2 long.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 10.0}

Before any card is revealed, the expected sum of the two cards is about 13.8, so I'm centring my quote there with a fairly wide spread.

**Fair value**
- The deck totals 0·4 + 2 + 3·4 + 6 + 7·4 + 11·4 + 15·4 = 152 over 22 cards.
- That is about 6.91 per card, so the two-card sum averages about 13.8.
- The sum's standard deviation is about 7.2, so the value could land well away from 13.8.

**How many counterparties are informed (alpha)**
- In round 1 there was no trade at a 4.5 bid. An informed counterparty would have sold there, since the value was 3, so that counterparty was a noise trader.
- The sale at 3 must also have been a noise trader. An informed one values the contract at exactly 3 and would not sell at 3.
- The sales at 8.8 and 4.5 fit either type. This points to a moderate alpha, most likely 0.5.

Because a meaningful share of counterparties may know the value, I keep the spread wide at about 9.6.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 18.6}

Round 2 so far: the first quote (9 / 18.6) drew no trade, which tells me little. Fair value is still about 13.8, so I'm keeping the quote wide and nearly the same.

**Fair value.** The deck's 22 cards add up to 152, so the average card is about 6.91. Two cards are dealt, so the expected sum is about **13.8**.

**Estimate of alpha from round 1.** For each alpha I computed how likely the four round-1 outcomes were:
- At bid 3 with settlement 3, an informed trader would not sell. So the sale at 3 must have come from a noise trader, which happens only about 12.5% of the time. That makes alpha = 0.9 unlikely.
- At bid 4.5 with settlement 3, an informed trader would have sold. So the no-trade at 4.5 / 13 points to a noise trader there.
- Combining all four outcomes, the posterior is roughly 0.34 for alpha = 0.05, 0.60 for alpha = 0.5, and 0.06 for alpha = 0.9. The expected alpha is about **0.36**, which is a meaningful informed share.

**Round 2 so far.** The no-trade at 9 / 18.6 hints that the sum may lie between 9 and 18.6, but the effect on fair value is small.

**Why stay wide.** The sum of two cards is widely spread, with a standard deviation of about 7. With roughly a third of counterparties informed, a tight quote would be picked off. Edges about 4.5–5 points from fair value still trade with noise traders around 20% of the time on each side.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 18.5}

Card 1 is 0, so the settlement equals card 2.

**Distribution of card 2 before using trades.** The remaining 21 cards are:
- three 0s, one 2, four 3s and one 6
- four 7s, four 11s and four 15s

Their mean is 152/21 ≈ 7.24.

**Evidence about alpha.** Round 1 looked heavily informed: they sold at 8.8 and 4.5 into a low settlement of 3. That makes alpha = 0.5 or 0.9 the likely cases.

**What the round 2 sale tells me.** In stage 1 the fair value was about 13.8. A noise trader sells at 9.2 only about 23% of the time. An informed trader sells only if the total is below 9.2, which means card 2 is 7 or less.
- Taking alpha as roughly 0.7, the chance of that sale is about 0.77 if card 2 is 7 or less. It is only about 0.07 if card 2 is 11 or 15.
- Thirteen cards are 7 or less and eight are 11 or 15. Weighting each group by those likelihoods gives roughly 95% that card 2 is one of {0, 2, 3, 6, 7}.
- My posterior expected value is therefore about 4.2.

**Ask.** I'll sell at 7.1. This is just above 7, so an informed trader holding a 7 won't lift it. Informed traders buy only if card 2 is 11 or 15, which is about a 5% chance. Noise buyers, centred near the public fair value, should hit it often, at a good edge over my estimate of about 4.2.

**Bid.** I'll bid low at 1.0. At that price an informed seller only trades if card 2 is 0, and I'm already long 1 unit.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 7.1}

With the first card at 0, the contract now settles at the value of card 2 alone. The remaining card values are bimodal: low (0 to 3), middle (6 to 7) and high (11 to 15).

**Estimating alpha.** Round 1 had at least two clearly noise-driven events:
- At quote 2, there was no trade even though an informed trader would have sold.
- At quote 4, someone sold at a bid of 3 when the value was exactly 3.

That makes alpha = 0.9 unlikely, so alpha is most likely 0.05 or 0.5.

**Estimating card 2.** This round's trades conflict.
- The sale at 9.2 in stage 1 points to a low value.
- The buy at 7.1 points to a high value.

So at least one of those trades was noise. My rough posterior for card 2 is:

| Group | Values | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| Low | 0, 2, 3 | about 0.34 |
| Middle | 6, 7 | about 0.21 |
| High | 11, 15 | about 0.44 |

That puts the fair value at about 7.7.

**Choosing the quote.** This is the last quote of the round and my position is flat. Because the distribution is bimodal, a wide quote does best:
- An ask around 13.5 is hit by informed traders only if the value is 15, and they gain at most 1.5 then. Noise buyers still trade there about 18% of the time.
- A bid around 2.5 is hit by informed traders only if the value is 0 or 2. The edge on noise sellers stays large.

The expected profit is roughly +0.5 on each side.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value: the average card is 152/22 ≈ 6.91, so the expected sum of two cards is about 13.8. The sum is widely spread, with a standard deviation of roughly 7.7.

What past trades say about the share of informed traders (alpha):
- At least three past trades could not have come from an informed counterparty, so they were noise traders:
  - Round 1 quote 2: no trade, although an informed trader would have sold at 4.5 with the value at 3.
  - Round 1 quote 4: they sold at 3 when the value was 3, so the trader's valuation was below 3.

{"bid": 9.3, "ask": 18.3}

The first trade this round, a sale at my bid of 9.3, is evidence that the sum is low.

**Prior and two cases.** Before any trading, the expected sum of two cards is 13.8 (each card averages 152/22 ≈ 6.9). The 231 possible two-card hands split into:

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 13.0}

Card 1 is 0, so the settlement equals card 2. The 21 cards left have a mean of about 7.24.

- Quote 1: they sold to me at 9.3. Quote 2: they did not trade at a bid of 6 and an ask of 13.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 7.4}

- **Quote 2:** no trade at 6 / 13. An informed trader stays out only if card 2 is 6, 7 or 11, so this favours those three values.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 12}

With card 1 = 4, the contract settles at 4 plus card 2, so it can only be 7, 10, 11, 13, 15 or 16. The prior mean is 4 + 127/14 ≈ 13.07.

**How informed are the counterparties?** The history points strongly to alpha = 0.05.

**What last quote's buy at 15.7 says.** Only a card 2 of 12 gives a value (16) above 15.7, so an informed trader would buy only then. A noise trader buys at 15.7 about 23% of the time. With alpha ≈ 0.05, the chance that card 2 is 12 rises from 0.29 to about 0.33. That puts fair value near 0.33 × 16 + 0.67 × 11.9 ≈ 13.2.

**Choosing the quote.** This is the last quote and my -2 position settles at the value either way, so inventory doesn't matter. Against noise with a standard deviation of 3.5, the profit-maximising edge is about 2.6 on each side.
- An ask of 16.0 means an informed trader never buys, since the value cannot exceed 16.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 14 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 2 cards worth 7, 4 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 11. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
I quoted a wide market around the expected value, because the share of informed traders (alpha) is unknown and the settlement distribution is lumpy.

**Fair value.** The average card value is (0·4 + 7·2 + 9·4 + 11·4)/14 = 94/14 ≈ 6.71. Three cards therefore have an expected sum of about 20.1. The standard deviation of the sum is about 7.

**Shape of the distribution.** It is clustered by how many 0-cards are dealt:
- **No zeros** (about 33%): the sum is roughly 23–33, averaging about 28.
- **One zero** (about 49%): the sum is roughly 14–22, averaging about 19.
- **Two or three zeros** (about 17%): the sum is under 12.

**Adverse selection.** Alpha could be as high as 0.9. Informed traders will pick off any price near the cluster edges, so I quote wide on both sides:
- **Ask at 27:** at 25–26, informed buyers would profit in most no-zero deals; 27 sits near the middle of that cluster.
- **Bid at 14:** low enough that one-zero hands near 14 don't make selling to me attractive.

Noise traders still cross a spread this wide occasionally, since their valuations vary with a standard deviation of 6.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 27}

Each card is worth 94/14 ≈ 6.71 on average, so three cards sum to about 20.1 in expectation, with a standard deviation of about 7. The last quote at 14/27 drew no trade, which gives a little evidence that the sum lies between 14 and 27. I'll centre my quote near 20.3 and tighten it slightly. That should still protect me against a possibly high share of informed traders.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 25}

With card 1 = 11 revealed, the remaining 13 cards are four 0s, two 7s, four 9s and three 11s. The two hidden cards can sum to 0, 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. So the contract's expected value is 11 + 2 × 83/13 ≈ 23.77.

**Possible settlement values**

| Value | 11 | 18 | 20 | 22 | 25 | 27 | 29 | 31 | 33 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ways (of 78) | 6 | 8 | 16 | 12 | 1 | 8 | 12 | 12 | 3 |

**Choosing the quote.** Alpha is still unknown; its prior average is about 0.48. The value comes in discrete steps, so it pays to quote just inside the gaps between those steps.

- **Bid 17.9.** This sits just below the 18 value. An informed trader only sells to me when the value is 11, which costs about 0.53 per quote. Noise traders sell to me about 16% of the time, with about 5.9 of edge each time.
- **Ask 30.9.** This sits just below the 31 value. The cost from informed traders is small, about 0.10 per quote. Noise traders buy from me about 12% of the time, with about 7.1 of edge each time.

Across the alpha prior, this pair has the best expected value of the options I compared, about +0.4. Tighter quotes, such as 21/26, lose money in expectation.

{"bid": 17.9, "ask": 30.9}

Quote 11 / 26 for this first quote of round 2: the ask a bit above fair value and the bid well below it.

**Fair value.** The average card is worth (4·0 + 2·7 + 4·9 + 4·11) / 14 = 94/14 ≈ 6.71. So the fair value of the 3-card sum is about 20.1. The spread is wide: the standard deviation is about 7.1, and the sum can be anywhere from 0 to 33.

**What we know about alpha.** Round 1 had no trades, so we have learned nothing about alpha. The prior mean is about 0.48. That means roughly half the counterparties may know the true sum.

**Ask side.** For each candidate ask I compared the expected noise-trader profit with the expected loss to informed traders. I counted the high-sum combinations exactly out of the 364 possible hands.

| Ask | Net expected edge per quote |
|---|---|
| 25 | about 0.01 |
| 26 | about 0.12 |
| 27 | about 0.20 |

**Bid side.** The low tail is heavy because four of the cards are 0, so the bid has to sit well below fair value.

| Bid | Net expected edge per quote |
|---|---|
| 14 | about 0.05 |
| 12 | about 0.10 |
| 11 | about 0.12 |
| 10 | about 0.11 |

The bid is set at 11, the best value in the table. The ask is set at 26, not 27, which is a judgement call that gives up some expected edge on the ask. Round 1 had no trades at roughly 14–16 / 25–27, so a slightly tighter ask improves the chance of a trade and of learning something about alpha.

{"bid": 11, "ask": 26}

I'm quoting a bid of 16 and an ask of 25, wide enough to protect against informed traders while still catching some noise trades.

- **Fair value:** the average card is worth (4·0 + 2·7 + 4·9 + 4·11)/14 = 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so the expected 3-card sum is about 20.1.
- **Shape of the outcome:** the sum is lumpy and skewed.
  - About 33% of deals contain no zero card, giving sums of roughly 25–33.
  - About 49% contain exactly one zero, giving sums of roughly 14–22.
  - About 17% contain two or more zeros, giving sums of 11 or less.
- **What the quotes so far tell me:** no trades yet, so I have learned little about how many counterparties are informed (alpha). A noise trader centred on 20.1 with standard deviation 6 would rarely fall outside 11–26, so the last miss is unsurprising.
- **Adverse selection:** if alpha is high, informed traders hit me on the extremes.
  - At an ask of 25, they buy mainly when the deal has no zeros.
  - At a bid of 16, they sell mainly on deals with two or more zeros.
- **Why this width:** these quotes keep that risk limited while still giving noise traders a reasonable chance to trade.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 25}

**Fair value**
- The remaining 13 cards are three 0s, two 7s, four 9s and four 11s. Their total is 94, so the average card is about 7.23.
- The expected sum of two cards is about 14.5.

**Bid 10, ask 19, about 4.5 either side of 14.5**

- **Bid side:** an informed trader sells only when the value is below 10, which means 0, 7 or 9. The expected cost per informed arrival is about 0.77.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 19}

Card 1 is 0, so the contract settles at the sum of the two hidden cards. Before the last trade, the expected value of the two cards was about 14.5.

Someone then bought from me at 19. An informed buyer at 19 means the value is 20 (9+11) or 22 (11+11). Round 1 had no trades at all, which leans towards a high share of informed traders. Taking that into account, my updated fair value is roughly 18.

For the ask, 22.1 is above the highest possible value of 22. So only noise traders can buy there, and that sale earns about 4 on average.

For the bid, 15 keeps informed sellers to cases where the value is 14 or less. That looks unlikely now, given the buy at 19. Noise traders still sell there fairly often, at about 3 below fair value.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 22.1}

Fair value before any card is revealed is about 20.1, so I'm quoting roughly symmetric around it at 15 / 25.3.

**Fair value.** The deck holds 14 cards with values 0, 0, 0, 0, 7, 7, 9, 9, 9, 9, 11, 11, 11, 11.
- The average card is 94/14 ≈ 6.71.
- The expected sum of 3 cards is about 20.14.
- The sum's standard deviation is about 7.1.

- In five of the six quotes where the settlement value 20 was known, it sat inside my spread. An informed trader would not have traded there, so those quotes say little about alpha.
- The one trade was a buy at 19 in round 2, after card 1 = 0. Public fair value was then about 14.5.
  - A noise trader buys there only about 23% of the time.
  - An informed trader buys for sure, since the settlement of 20 was above 19.

**Quote.** With alpha likely high and a wide settlement range, being picked off is costly, so I keep the spread wide. I set it a little below the spread of about 9 that drew no trades in both rounds' second stage-1 quote.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 25.3}

The public fair value is now about 25.0. I'm already short 1, so I'll widen my quotes around that.

- **Prior value:** the mean card is 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so before any trade the expected sum of 3 cards is about 20.1.
- **If the buyer was informed:** they bought at 25.3, so the true sum must be at least 27. The possible sums are 27, 29, 31 and 33, which averages about 28.9. This happens with probability about 0.275 per quote.
- **If the buyer was a noise trader:** their valuation had to exceed 25.3, which has probability about 0.20. That buy says nothing about the value, which stays at 20.1.
- **Who was it?** Weighting each possible alpha (0.05, 0.5, 0.9) by how likely this buy was under it gives about a 56% chance the buyer was informed.
- **Fair value:** 0.56 × 28.9 + 0.44 × 20.1 ≈ 25.0.

I'm short 1 and there is upside risk if informed traders keep buying. So I quote a wide spread centred slightly above 25.

{"bid": 21.5, "ask": 29.5}

Card 1 = 11 leaves 13 cards: four 0s, two 7s, four 9s and three 11s. On the card count alone, the expected settlement is about 23.8. The trading history pushes that up.

- **Stage 1 buy at 25.3:** an informed trader buys there only if the settlement is 27 or more. A noise trader buys there only about 20% of the time.
- **No trade at 21.5 / 29.5:** an informed trader stays out only if the settlement is between 22 and 29.
- **Round 2 buy at 19 (settled 20):** this fits an informed trader, so a high alpha is more likely.

Combining this evidence gives roughly these weights for alpha: 0.05 about 8%, 0.5 about 29%, 0.9 about 63%. The settlement is most likely 27 or 29, with some weight on 31 or 33. The fair value comes out at about 27.8.

I'll quote a bid below 27 and an ask above 29. That way informed traders holding the most likely values (27 and 29) won't trade with me. I still earn the spread from noise traders around the 27.8 fair value. The main remaining risk is the 31 or 33 cases, where I lose a little at the ask.

{"bid": 26.5, "ask": 29.9}

With card 1 = 11 and earlier trade evidence pointing to an informed buyer, I expect the round to settle at 27 or 29, with fair value about 28.1.

**Remaining deck.** Thirteen cards are left: four 0s, two 7s, four 9s and three 11s. With no other information, the expected total is 11 + 2 × 83/13 ≈ 23.8.

**What this round's trades suggest.**
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at 25.3, well above the prior fair value of about 20.1. A noise trader does that only about 19% of the time, so this was likely an informed buyer, meaning the total is above 25.3.
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded at 21.5 / 29.5. If informed, the total is between 21.5 and 29.5.
- **Quote 3:** nobody traded at 26.5 / 29.9. If informed, the total is between 26.5 and 29.9.
- **Alpha:** earlier rounds suggest it is 0.5 or 0.9, not 0.05.
- **Possible totals:** the only totals consistent with all three facts are 27 (card values 7+9) and 29 (7+11 or 9+9). They carry most of the posterior weight.

**Quote choice.** A bid of 27 and an ask of 29 means an informed trader holding 27 or 29 will not trade with me. Only noise traders, or the rare outlier totals, will trade, and each noise trade earns about +1 against fair value.

{"bid": 27.0, "ask": 29.0}

With no cards revealed, the fair value is the expected three-card sum. Each card averages 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so the sum averages about 20.1. The value is spread widely, from 0 up to 33, with a lot of weight at 27–31 and at sums near 11 that include a zero.

The history suggests many counterparties are informed (alpha is likely 0.5 or 0.9). Both trades so far went in the direction an informed trader would choose: a buy at 19 with settlement 20, and a buy at 25.3 with settlement 29. Every non-trade happened with the settlement value inside my spread.

I'll quote wide so informed traders only trade with me in the tails, and only lose me a few points when they do.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 29.5}

Before any card is revealed, the fair value is about 21.3. My bid of 15.5 and ask of 27.5 are set so that an informed trader trades with me only on the rare extreme sums (14 or 29).

**Fair value**
- The average card is worth 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so three cards average about 20.14 before any information.
- The no-trade at my last quote (12 / 29.5) shifts this up a little. An informed trader would have traded if the sum were below 12 or above 29.5.

**Share of informed traders**

- A noise trader had only about a 20% chance of making each of those trades.
- No informed trader was ever forced to trade at my other quotes.
- So it is likely that most counterparties are informed (alpha is probably high), and I should keep the quote wide.

- Possible sums between 12 and 29.5 are 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 23, 25, 27 and 29.
- A bid of 15.5 stays above the rare sum of 14 but below 16, which is common.
- An ask of 27.5 stays above 27, which is common, so only the sum of 29 would make an informed trader buy, and that loses me just 1.5.
- Noise traders still trade with me sometimes, and those trades are profitable.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 27.5}

Card 1 = 7, so the remaining 13 cards are four 0s, one 7, four 9s and four 11s. The settlement can only be 29 if the other two cards are both 11s (prior chance 6/78 ≈ 8%). Otherwise the most likely sums are around 20.

- If the informed share is 0.9, the chance the settlement is 29 is about 0.87.
- If it is 0.5, the chance is about 0.45.

- **Bid at 25.5:** an informed trader only sells to me if the settlement is 25 or below. Noise sellers still give a good edge, and a fill would reduce my short of 1 unit.

{"bid": 25.5, "ask": 29.0}

- An informed counterparty with a value of 29 explains both observations: the buy at 27.5, and no trade at last quote's 25.5 / 29.
- If the counterparty was a noise trader, the buy is much less likely.
- Putting these together, the chance the total is 29 is about 97%. The main alternative is 27.

**My quote.** A trader who knows the total is 29 won't trade with a bid below 29 or an ask above 29. I'll quote wide around 29 to pick up any noise trades at a profit. If the total is actually 27, the bid of 27 still won't lose money.

{"bid": 27, "ask": 30.5}

Without a reveal, the fair value is about 20.1: each card averages 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so three cards average about 20.14.

Every trade so far is consistent with an informed counterparty:
- **Round 2:** they bought at 19 and it settled at 20.
- **Round 3:** they bought at 25.3 and it settled at 29.
- **Round 4:** they bought at 27.5 and it settled at 29.

Across many fairly tight quotes there were no trades that looked like noise. That makes a high alpha (0.5 or 0.9) likely, so I'll keep the spread wide.

- **Low end:** any hand with two or more zeros sums to 11 or less. That happens in 64 of 364 hands, so a bid at 11 is rarely hit by an informed seller.

{"bid": 11, "ask": 30}

The expected sum is about 20.1, since each card averages 94/14 ≈ 6.71.

**What alpha looks like.** All three past trades were buys well above the public fair value, and each settled above the price paid. That pattern points strongly to informed counterparties, so I put alpha near 0.8.

**What the stage-1 no-trades tell me.** An informed trader would have traded at (15, 26) unless the total was between 15 and 26. Given card 1 = 9, that leaves totals of 16, 18, 20, 23 or 25. Weighting those against the outside totals (9, 27, 29, 31), the posterior fair value is about 20. Most of the probability sits at 16–20, with a tail at 25 and some outside mass at 27–31.

The bid is best around 15–15.9, because a bid above 16 gets hit by informed traders holding a total of 16.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 26}

Each card averages 94/14 ≈ 6.71, so three cards have an expected sum of about 20.1. That is the fair value with nothing revealed.

**How informed the counterparties seem.** Every trade so far went against me, and the settlement confirmed the counterparty knew the value:
- Round 2: bought at 19 when fair was about 14.5. It settled at 20.
- Round 3: bought at 25.3. It settled at 29.
- Round 4: bought at 27.5. It settled at 29.

There were also many quotes with no trade, where noise traders with a standard deviation of 6 would often have traded. Both points suggest alpha is probably high (0.9), so I should quote wide where the tails of the sum are thin.

**Where the tails are.** The sum has a lumpy distribution:

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 6, 10.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 4, 9, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
The prior expected maximum is about 9.43, and the chance that the settlement is 12 is 1/3. Someone bought at 11.8. Averaged over the possible alpha values, Bayes' rule puts the chance of a 12 at about 0.80, so the public fair value is now about 11.2.

- **Ask at 12.0:** The contract can never settle above 12, so an informed trader will never buy there. Only noise traders can hit it, which makes this ask riskless.
- **Bid at 10.0:** Any value below 12 is at most 10, so this bid limits adverse selection to the cases where the value is below 10. That has about a 12% chance under the current estimate.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 12.0}

Die 3 showed 12, and dice 1 and 2 can roll at most 10. So the contract settles at **12** for certain, and everyone knows it.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 12. They will not trade as long as my bid is at or below 12 and my ask is at or above 12.
- **Noise traders** value it at 12 plus normal noise with standard deviation 2.1. Only they will trade with me.
- **Choosing the spread:** the expected profit on each side is e × P(noise > e), where e is the distance from 12. This is largest at about e ≈ 0.75 × 2.1 ≈ 1.6.
- **Quote:** that gives a bid of 10.4 and an ask of 13.6. Each side earns an expected 1.6 × 0.224 ≈ 0.36 per noise trader.
- **Position:** I'm short 1, so I can still buy or sell one unit either way within the limit.

{"bid": 10.4, "ask": 13.6}

The fair value before anything is revealed is about 9.43, so I'll quote a bid of 8.0 and an ask of 11.6. The spread is wide because informed traders could be a large share of counterparties.

**Expected value of the maximum.** I used E[max] = Σₖ P(max ≥ k). The chance that the maximum is below k is the product of the three dice's chances of being below k:

| k | P(max < k) |
|---|---|
| 1–3 | 0 |
| 4 | 1/36 |
| 5 | 1/24 |
| 6 | 1/8 |
| 7 | 3/16 |
| 8 | 3/16 |
| 9 | 1/4 |
| 10 | 5/12 |
| 11 | 2/3 |
| 12 | 2/3 |

These sum to about 2.57, so E[max] ≈ 12 − 2.57 ≈ **9.43**.

**Shape of the distribution.**
- The maximum is 12 with probability 1/3 (die 3 shows 12).
- It is 10 with probability 1/4 and 9 with probability 1/6.
- The rest lies at 8 or below.

**What round 1 tells me.** There was only one trade: a buy at 11.8 that settled at 12. That fits an informed buyer but tells me little about alpha.

**Setting the quotes.**
- **Ask:** At 11.6, informed traders buy only when the value is 12 (1/3 chance), costing me 0.4 each time. Noise traders buy about 15% of the time, gaining me roughly 2.2.
- **Bid:** At 8.0, informed traders sell only when the value is 7 or less (about 3/16 chance). Noise traders sell when their valuation falls about 1.4 below fair value.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The fair value is 10.85 (0.31 heads per flip × 7 flips × 5). Settlement can only be a multiple of 5, so I quote just inside those values to limit what informed traders can take from me.

- **Bid 4.9:** an informed trader sells only if the value is 0, which has about a 12% chance. A noise trader sells with about a 17% chance and pays roughly 6 below fair. This side has positive expected profit at the average alpha.
- **Ask 15.1 was rejected:** informed traders would buy at a value of 20 or more, about a 19% chance. At the average alpha, the expected loss to them is slightly larger than the expected gain from noise traders.
- **Ask 19.9:** an informed trader buys only if the value is 25 or more, about an 8% chance. The noise-trader gain is a bit larger than that, so the expected profit is slightly positive.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 19.9}

Before the first quote my fair value was about 10.85: the expected chance of heads is 0.31, so 7 flips give about 2.17 heads, times 5. After the buy at 19.9 my estimate is now about 19.

**Who bought at 19.9.**
- An informed trader buys at 19.9 only if the coin shows 4 or more heads. That has a prior chance of about 0.19.
- A noise trader values the contract at 10.85 plus noise with standard deviation 6.3. It buys at 19.9 only about 7.5% of the time.
- So the buy makes a high informed share (alpha) more likely. My estimates for alpha = 0.05, 0.5 and 0.9 move from 1/3 each to about 0.21, 0.34 and 0.46.
- Overall, the chance this buyer was informed is about 0.70.

**Fair value now.**
- If the buyer was informed, there were 4 or more heads. Given that, the expected heads are about 4.5, so the value is about 22.6.
- If the buyer was noise, the buy tells me nothing and the value stays about 10.85.
- Weighting these, 0.70 × 22.6 + 0.30 × 10.85 ≈ 19.1.

**Quote.** The informed share is probably high and the value is split into two clusters (roughly 20 and up, or near 11). So I keep the spread wide around 19, leaning slightly toward buying because I'm short.
- An ask of 25 only gets taken by an informed trader if there are 5 or more heads.
- A bid of 14 only gets hit by an informed trader if there are 2 or fewer heads (value 10 or less), which can only happen if the earlier buyer was noise.

{"bid": 14.0, "ask": 25.0}

The quote is bid 17.5, ask 25.0. Fair value is about 20.4, and I'm keeping the spread wide because the counterparties look mostly informed.

**Flips.** Flip 1 = 0 and flip 2 = 1 update the coin to roughly P(0.2) = 0.41, P(0.3) = 0.21 and P(0.5) = 0.38. Taken alone, that gives an expected head count of about 2.7, or a value of about 13.4.

**Trades.**
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at 19.9 when fair value was about 10.9. A noise trader does that only about 8% of the time. An informed trader does it whenever there are at least 4 heads (value 20 or more).
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded at 14 / 25. An informed trader would stay out at those prices only if there were 3, 4 or 5 heads.

Putting the flips and trades together:
- **Heads:** roughly H=4 at 63%, H=5 at 25% and H≤3 at 11%.
- **Fair value:** about 20.4.
- **Alpha:** the share of informed traders now leans high, roughly 0.05 / 0.5 / 0.9 at 0.12 / 0.31 / 0.57.

**Quote choice.** The likely settlement values are 20 and 25, so I avoid quoting inside them.
- **Ask at 25.0:** an informed trader with value 25 won't buy, so only H=6 hurts me. A noise trader buys with about 23% probability and I earn about 4.6.
- **Bid at 17.5:** an informed trader at value 20 or 25 won't sell to me. Noise sellers give me a decent edge. The main risk is the roughly 11% chance that H≤3.

The trade history moves this a lot:

An informed trader behaving this way must have a settlement value of 20 or 25. Those are the only values consistent with all three quotes.

Weighting each alpha by how well it explains this history makes a high alpha very likely. My posterior on settlement is roughly:
- 20 with about 69%
- 25 with about 28%
- lower values with the small remainder

That gives an expected value of about 21.

- **Noise trader:** the valuation falls below 9.9, which happens about 29% of the time whatever the true value is.

**Updated fair value.** Averaging over the three possible values of alpha (mean about 0.48), the chance the value is low rises to about 0.61. Fair value is then about 0.61 × 3.4 + 0.39 × 17.9 ≈ 9.1.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 11 balls, each red or blue. Each ball was independently painted red with probability 0.3. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:

- **Ask 50:** an informed buyer trades only if the value is above 50, so 60 or more, which has probability about 8%. Its expected loss is about 1.0. A noise buyer trades with probability about 9.5% and gains about 17, roughly 1.6.

Both sides have positive expected profit for any likely alpha. The quotes also sit exactly on value levels, so ties at 20 or 50 do not trade.

- **Ask at 50:** an informed trader buys only if the value is 60 or more, which happens about 8% of the time. That costs roughly 1.0 per informed arrival. A noise trader buys about 9.5% of the time at a 17-point edge, worth roughly 1.6. At the prior average alpha of about 0.48, the ask has positive expected profit. An ask of 41 would lose money on average, and 60 earns less.
- **Bid at 20:** an informed trader sells only if the value is 0 or 10, about 11% of the time. That costs roughly 1.3 per informed arrival. A noise trader sells about 16% of the time at a 13-point edge, worth roughly 2.1. Net, the bid is positive. A bid of 30 would be clearly negative.

game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 3, 3, 6, 8, 10, 10, 12, 12.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 2, 7, 9.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 3, 6, 6, 7, 11.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.
