Fair value before any reveal is the expected gap between the two dealt cards.

**Fair value.** Take each gap between neighbouring card values. Multiply it by the number of cards below the gap and the number of cards above it, then add these up.

| Gap | Size | Cards below | Cards above | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4→5 | 1 | 2 | 18 | 36 |
| 5→8 | 3 | 3 | 17 | 153 |
| 8→9 | 1 | 4 | 16 | 64 |
| 9→10 | 1 | 6 | 14 | 84 |
| 10→12 | 2 | 10 | 10 | 200 |
| 12→13 | 1 | 14 | 6 | 84 |
| 13→14 | 1 | 16 | 4 | 64 |

The total is 685. There are C(20,2) = 190 possible pairs, so the expected settlement is 685 / 190 ≈ 3.6.

**Spread.** The settlement value varies a lot: it can be anywhere from 0 to 10, and it is 0 about 11% of the time. The share of informed traders is unknown and could be as high as 0.9. So I'll quote a fairly wide spread around 3.6, about 1.3 on each side.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 4.9}

A buy at 4.9 is meaningful evidence that the settlement is high, so I am moving my quotes up a lot and keeping them wide.

**Prior value.** Over the 190 possible pairs of dealt cards, the sum of |difference| is 685. So the prior expected settlement is 685 / 190 ≈ 3.6.

**What the buy at 4.9 tells me.**
- 60 of the 190 pairs (31.6%) have a difference of at least 5. Their average difference is about 7.0. The other pairs average about 2.0.
- A noise trader would buy at 4.9 with probability about 0.25, since that is P(3.6 + N(0, 1.9) > 4.9).
- An informed trader buys only when the value is above 4.9.

**Updated estimate.**
- I averaged the buy probability over the three possible alphas (0.05, 0.5, 0.9).
- That gives P(value ≥ 5 | buy) ≈ 0.69.
- The updated fair value is about 0.69 × 7.0 + 0.31 × 2.0 ≈ 5.4.

**Quote.** I am centring near 5.4 with a wide spread, because informed traders may be common. I lean slightly higher because I am already short one unit.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 6.8}

With card 1 = 10, my fair value for the contract is about 4.4, so I'm centering a wide quote there and leaning slightly upward because I'm short.

**Base case from the cards alone.** The other 19 cards give these outcomes for |card 2 − 10|:

| Value | Cards that give it | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 10 | 3 |
| 1 | 9 | 2 |
| 2 | 8 or 12 | 5 |
| 3 | 13 | 2 |
| 4 | 14 | 4 |
| 5 | 5 | 1 |
| 6 | 4 | 2 |

From the cards alone the expected value is 51/19 ≈ 2.68.

**What the trades tell me.**
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at my ask of 4.9. An informed trader only does that if the value is 5 or 6.
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded at 4.2 / 6.8. That fits a value of 5–6, because an informed trader would have sold to me at 4.2 if the value were 4 or less.

**Updating.**
- I averaged over the three possible informed shares (0.05, 0.5, 0.9). Those two observations are about 9 times more likely if the value is 5–6 than if it is lower.
- That moves the probability of a 5–6 outcome from 3/19 to about 63%.
- The posterior mean is therefore about 0.63 × 5.67 + 0.37 × 2.13 ≈ 4.4.

**The quote.** There is a real chance that informed traders dominate, so I'm keeping the spread wide.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.6}

Card 1 is 10, so the settlement is |card 2 − 10|. Of the remaining 19 cards, the distance from 10 works out as:

| Value | Cards | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | three 10s | 3/19 |
| 1 | two 9s | 2/19 |
| 2 | the 8 and four 12s | 5/19 |
| 3 | two 13s | 2/19 |
| 4 | four 14s | 4/19 |
| 5 | the 5 | 1/19 |
| 6 | two 4s | 2/19 |

That gives a fair value of 51/19 ≈ 2.68.

This is the last quote of the round, so I only care about this quote's own profit. Alpha is uncertain, and the buy at 4.9 in stage 1 hints that some counterparties are informed. So I want quotes that hold up even if alpha is high, while still earning from noise traders.

**Bid side:**
- An informed trader sells only when the value is below my bid. Bidding very low limits that to the value-0 outcomes.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((bid − 2.68)/1.9), and I gain 2.68 − bid each time.
- A bid of about 0.3 gives roughly +0.1 expected profit at mid-range alpha, and the loss is small if alpha is 0.9.

**Ask side:**
- At 5.5, an informed trader only buys when the value is 6 (2/19 chance), losing me 0.5 each time.
- A noise trader buys about 7% of the time, and I gain about 2.8 each time.
- That is roughly +0.07 expected at mid-range alpha, and the quote stays fairly robust if alpha is high.

{"bid": 0.3, "ask": 5.5}

No trade at 2.3 / 5 last quote, so fair value is still about 3.6. I'm keeping a fairly wide spread around it because I don't know what fraction of traders are informed.

**Expected range before any card is revealed**
- Over all 190 possible two-card pairs, the differences add up to 685.
- So the expected range is 685 / 190 ≈ 3.61.

**Reading the last quote**
- Nobody traded at 2.3 / 5.
- If the trader was informed, the value is probably between 2.3 and 5. Ranges of 3, 4 and 5 are fairly common, so this leaves fair value near 3.6.

**Quote**
- I quote 2.5 / 4.8, roughly centred on 3.6.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 4.8}

Card 1 is 14, so the contract settles at 14 − card 2. The possible values are 10, 9, 6, 5, 4, 2, 1 and 0. The prior mean is about 3.74.

**How informed the traders seem.** In round 1 someone bought at 4.9 and the contract settled at 5. At every other quote that round, an informed trader would also have stayed out. That fits a high alpha, so I put my estimate at about 0.75.

**What this round's trades say.** In stage 1, nobody traded at 2.3/5. Then someone bought at 4.8. For an informed trader, that pattern only happens if the value is exactly 5. Updating on this gives roughly:
- value 5: about 65%
- value 4: about 12%
- value 6 or more: about 15%
- value 2 or less: about 8%

The fair value comes out around 5.1.

**Choosing the quote.** The values are whole numbers, so I can place prices to avoid some informed trades:
- A bid of exactly 4.0 means an informed trader with value 4 won't sell to me.
- An ask of exactly 6.0 means an informed trader with value 6 won't buy from me.

With these prices, informed traders only hit me when the value is 9 or more, or 2 or less. Noise traders still trade on both sides at about a 1-point edge.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.0}

Card 1 is 14, so the settlement value is 14 minus card 2. Before the last trade the fair value was about 3.7, but someone sold to me at 4, which points to a lower card-2 gap. That puts fair value now at about 2.5, and the likely values cluster at 0, 1 and 2. I'm quoting a fairly wide spread around that.

**Before the last trade.** Card 2 comes from the 19 cards left. The possible settlement values and their card counts are:

| Value | 10 | 9 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cards | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 3 |

The mean is 71/19 ≈ 3.74.

**Updating on the sell at 4.**
- An informed trader sells at 4 only if the value is below 4, which means a value of 0, 1 or 2.
- A noise trader sells at 4 about 55% of the time, whatever the value.

The updated fair value depends on how many traders are informed (alpha):

| Alpha | Fair value |
|---|---|
| 0.05 | ≈ 3.6 |
| 0.5 | ≈ 2.5 |
| 0.9 | ≈ 1.4 |

Weighting these by how likely each alpha is gives a fair value of about 2.5.

**The quote.**
- **Bid 1.0:** an informed trader would sell to me only when the value is 0.
- **Ask 4.1:** an informed trader would buy from me only when the value is 5 or more, which is now fairly unlikely.
- This keeps a spread around fair value against noise traders while limiting what informed traders can take.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.1}

Before any card is revealed, the expected range of the two cards is about 3.6. I'm quoting around that, wide, because I can't yet tell how many counterparties are informed.

**Expected settlement value**
- The deck has 20 cards, so there are 190 possible pairs of dealt cards.
- Adding up the difference between the two cards across every cross-value pair gives a total of 685.
- 685 / 190 ≈ 3.61.
- The outcomes are spread widely. A 0 settlement happens about 11% of the time (21 of 190 pairs), and a 10 is also possible.

**How many counterparties are informed (alpha)**
- In round 1, someone bought at 4.9 and the contract settled at 5. That is consistent with an informed trader.
- In round 2, someone bought at 4.8 and it settled at 0, so that buyer was noise.
- In round 2, someone sold at 4 and it settled at 0, which looks informed.
- The evidence is mixed, so I keep a wide spread around the mean of about 3.6.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 4.9}

The contract's unconditional expected value is about 3.6. The counterparty who just bought at 4.9 could have been informed, which pushes my fair value up to roughly 4.8–5.0.

**Unconditional value.** E|card1 − card2| works out to 685 / 190 ≈ 3.61. About 32% of deals settle at 5 or more, with a conditional mean of about 7.0.

**Effect of the buy at 4.9.**
- A noise trader buys there with probability about 25%.
- An informed trader buys only if the value is at least 5, which happens about 32% of the time.
- Past rounds give mixed evidence on alpha. In round 2, someone bought at 4.8 and the round settled at 0, so that buyer must have been a noise trader.
- Weighting the possible alpha values together gives a fair value of about 4.8–5.0.

**Quote.** I am short 1 and don't want much more short exposure, so I set the ask well above fair value. The bid is somewhat below fair to guard against an informed seller.

{"bid": 3.8, "ask": 6.2}

Card 1 is 9, so the fair value is about 3.9. I'm quoting an ask just above the maximum possible value and a bid well below fair value.

**Value distribution.** With card 1 = 9, these are the possible ranges across the 19 remaining cards:

| Range | Card 2 | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 9 | 1 |
| 1 | 8, 10 | 5 |
| 3 | 12 | 4 |
| 4 | 5, 13 | 3 |
| 5 | 4, 14 | 6 |

The unconditional mean is about 3.1.

**Update from this round's trade.** A counterparty bought at 4.9 in stage 1. An informed trader buys at 4.9 only if the value is 5, so this trade shifts weight toward a range of 5.

**Estimate of alpha.**
- Two trades fit informed traders: round 1's buy at 4.9 settled at 5, and round 2's sell at 4 settled at 0.
- One trade must have been noise: round 2's buy at 4.8 settled at 0.
- So alpha is probably moderate, and the fair value is about 3.9–4.1.

**Quote.**
- **Ask at 5.1:** this is above the maximum possible value of 5, so informed traders can never buy from me. Noise traders still buy fairly often, and that also helps reduce my short position.
- **Bid at 2.7:** informed traders would sell to me only when the value is 0 or 1. Noise traders well below fair value would also sell, giving some edge.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 5.1}

Card 1 is 9, so my fair value for this contract is about 4.2, and I'm quoting bid 4.0 / ask 5.1.

**Prior given card 1 = 9.** The contract settles at |card 2 − 9|. Over the 19 remaining cards, the possible values and how many cards give each are:

| Settlement value | 0 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of cards | 1 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 6 |

That gives a prior mean of about 3.1.

**Updating on this round's trades.**
- At quote 1, a counterparty bought at 4.9. If they were informed, the value is at least 5, so 5 is the only possible value.
- At quote 3, nobody traded at 2.7 / 5.1. An informed trader would have sold if the value were 0 or 1. So no trade points towards values of 3, 4 or 5.

**Read on alpha.** Earlier rounds are mixed. Some trades look informed: the 4.9 buy in round 1 and the sale at 4 in round 2. One clearly isn't: the 4.8 buy in round 2, which settled at 0. My working estimate is alpha around 0.5.

**Posterior.** With alpha around 0.5, weight shifts heavily onto a value of 5. The posterior mean is about 4.4, or lower if alpha is small. I'll use a fair value of about 4.2.

**Quote.**
- I'm short 1, so buying back at 4.0 is acceptable.
- An ask of 5.1 avoids selling to an informed buyer when the value is 5.
- Noise traders whose valuation is above 5.1 still pay me a good edge.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 5.1}

Before any card is revealed, the expected range is 685/190 ≈ 3.61. I got this by summing |a−b| over all 190 possible pairs of dealt cards.

**Downside risk:**
- About 43% of deals settle at 2 or below:
  - range 0: 21/190
  - range 1: 28/190
  - range 2: 32/190
- An informed seller would hit a bid near 2.3 fairly often, so I keep the bid low.

**Upside risk:**
- My ask near 4.9 was hit at the first quote in all three earlier rounds.
- Two of those rounds settled at 5.
- A noise trader needs a draw about 0.7 standard deviations above fair value to buy there, so three out of three fills hints that alpha may not be small.
- I nudge the ask up slightly.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 5.0}

The fair value has dropped a lot because someone sold to me at 2.2, so I'm quoting about **1.1 / 3.8**, pulled down slightly because I'm already long one.

**Starting value.** The contract pays the gap between the two dealt cards. Its average over all possible pairs is 685/190 ≈ 3.6.

**What the sale tells me.** The trade at 2.2 makes a low gap more likely.
- An informed trader sells only if the gap is 0, 1 or 2. That happens in 85 of the 190 pairs, about 45%. When it happens, the average gap is about 1.2.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((2.2 − 3.6)/1.9) ≈ 23%. That trade says nothing about the gap.
- The past trades are mixed, so I treat alpha as roughly 0.5. Weighting the two cases, the expected gap is now about 2.0–2.5. I use about 2.3.

**Quote.** I'm long one at 2.2, so I lean slightly lower to make selling more likely than buying. The quote stays fairly wide because informed traders may be common.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.8}

Card 1 is 12, so the settlement value is |12 − card 2|. My estimate of that value is about 0.85, and my quote is bid 0, ask 1.9.

**Remaining 19 cards:** 2×4, 1×5, 1×8, 2×9, 4×10, 3×12, 2×13, 4×14.
- Settlement 0 needs a 12 (3 cards) and 1 needs a 13 (2 cards).
- Settlement 2 needs a 10 or 14 (8 cards).
- The other 6 cards give 3–8.
- Before using this round's trades, the expected value is 51/19 ≈ 2.7.

**What the trades say:** Counterparties sold to me at 2.2 and again at 1.1.
- An informed trader would make both sells if the true value is 0 or 1.
- A noise trader would need to be well below the public fair value twice.
- So the value is very likely 0 or 1, especially if alpha is moderate or high.

**Estimating alpha from earlier rounds:**
- In round 3 someone bought at 5.1 when the contract settled at 5, which only a noise trader would do. That makes alpha = 0.9 less likely.
- Combining that with this round's two sells, my posterior is about 15% / 52% / 33% on alpha = 0.05 / 0.5 / 0.9.
- That gives an expected settlement value of about 0.85.

**Quote:** I am long 2 at an average price of 1.65, above my estimate, so I want to sell.
- **Ask 1.9:** about 1 above fair. Noise traders still buy fairly often, and an informed trader buys only if the value is 2 or more, which is now unlikely.
- **Bid 0:** the value cannot go below 0, so an informed trader will never sell to me there. Only noise traders hit it, and that is profitable.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 1.9}

Card 1 is 12. The remaining 19 cards give these values: 0 (3 ways), 1 (2), 2 (8), 3 (2), 4 (1), 7 (1) and 8 (2). That makes the unconditional mean about 2.7.

This round's trading points to a low value:
- **Stage 1:** counterparties sold to me at 2.2 and again at 1.1.
- **Quote 3:** with an ask of 1.9, no one bought. An informed trader would have bought if the value were 2 or more.

Earlier rounds suggest alpha is moderate to high. Putting this together, almost all the probability is on a value of 0 or 1, with a posterior mean of about 0.5.

**Bid at 0:** informed traders never sell there, since the value is at least 0. Any fill comes from a noise trader, at no worse than fair. Going to +3 is fine.

**Ask at 1.0:** an informed trader holding a value of 1 won't lift it. Noise traders, valuing around 0.5, will sometimes buy, which lets me unload long inventory above its expected value.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.0}

Prior expected range is about 3.6 (685/190 over all card pairs). The no-trade at 2.3/4.9 suggests the value may be 3 or 4, but that leaves the mean near 3.6. Past fills look mixed: some match informed traders and some don't, so alpha is probably moderate. I'll keep a fairly wide quote centred near 3.6.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 4.8}

Card 1 is 13. Counting the 19 cards left, the prior expected spread is about 3.1. The possible values are 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 and 9.

**Evidence from this round's trades**
- At quote 1 there was no trade at 2.3/4.9. That points toward a value of 3 or 4.
- At quote 2 someone bought at 4.8. That points toward a value of 5, 8 or 9.

**What I'm assuming about alpha**
- The earlier rounds look like a mix of informed and noise trades, so I'm assuming alpha is moderate, around 0.5.
- On that assumption, my estimate of fair value is about 4–4.5. I put about 21% on a value of 0–1, 42% on 3–4, and 37% on 5–9.

**Quote**
- I'm already short 1, so I'll quote wide and sit slightly below my estimated fair value.
- At these prices, an informed trader would only hit me when the value is at the extremes: 0–1 on the bid side, 8–9 on the ask side.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 5.8}

Card 1 is 13 and I'm short 2. My quote is a bid of 8.0 and an ask of 9.0. That spread costs me nothing against an informed trader if the value is 8 or 9, which I think is very likely.

**Possible settlements.** The other 19 cards give these values for 13 minus card 2:

| Value | 9 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 1 | 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Card 2 | 4 | 5 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 12 or 14 | 13 |
| Number of cards | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 1 |

The average value before looking at trades is about 3.1.

**How many traders are informed.** Four earlier trades or non-trades happened where an informed trader would have acted differently, so most traders are not informed. Many other trades matched the settlement value, though, so a share of about half (alpha = 0.5) fits the history best.

**This round's trades.** Someone bought at 4.8 and then at 5.8.
- A noise trader valuing above 5.8 after the reveal is unlikely, at roughly 8%.
- An informed buyer at 5.8 needs the value to be 8 or 9, meaning card 2 is a 4 or a 5.
- With alpha around 0.5, the chance the value is 8 or 9 is about 93%. Within that, 9 is twice as likely as 8, so the expected value is about 8.2 to 8.3.

**The quote.**
- At a bid of 8.0, an informed trader holding value 8 will not sell to me.
- At an ask of 9.0, an informed trader holding value 9 will not buy from me.
- Noise traders around the public fair value can still trade on either side.
- A fill at the bid lowers my risk on the short position.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value here is about 3.6, and I'm quoting 2.3 bid / 4.9 ask, roughly ±1.3 around it.

**Expected range.** The expected value of the largest card minus the smallest, over all 190 possible two-card pairs, is 685/190 ≈ **3.6**. The outcomes are widely spread: about 11% of pairs settle at 0 (both cards the same value), and the largest possible range is 10.

**Informed share (alpha).** The history is mixed:
- Some trades look like noise traders. In round 2 someone bought at 4.8 and it settled at 0. In round 5 someone bought at 9 and it settled at exactly 9, which an informed trader would not do.
- Others look informed. In round 4 two sells, at 2.2 and 1.1, came before a settlement of 1.

So alpha is probably moderate (around 0.5). That calls for a fairly wide spread around the fair value. This matches the quotes I've used at this point in earlier rounds.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 4.9}

After the sell at 2.3, my estimate of fair value is about 2.0. I'm long 1 unit, so I'm quoting 0.8 / 3.0, roughly centred on that.

**Prior value.** Averaged over all 190 possible two-card pairs, the expected gap between the cards is 685/190 ≈ 3.6.

**What the history says about informed traders.**
- Most trades so far would also have made sense to someone who knew the settlement value, so the informed share is probably 0.5 or 0.9.
- Two events rule out every counterparty being informed:
  - In round 2 they bought at 4.8 and it settled at 0.
  - In round 5 nobody bought at 4.9 and it settled at 9.
- My rough weighting is about 0.6 on 0.5, 0.3 on 0.9 and 0.1 on 0.05.

**What this round's sell at 2.3 says.**
- An informed counterparty sells at 2.3 only if the value is 0, 1 or 2. That happens with probability 81/190 ≈ 0.43, and the average value in that case is about 1.14.
- A noise trader sells at 2.3 only about 25% of the time.
- So the sell pulls the expected value down. It is about 2.05 if the informed share is 0.5, about 1.3 if it is 0.9, and about 3.4 if it is 0.05.
- Weighting those gives roughly 2.0.

**Quote.** I'm quoting around about 2.0 with a moderately wide spread to protect against informed traders. The ask is kept slightly low so I'm more likely to sell off the long unit.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 3.0}

The revealed first card is 14, so settlement is 14 minus card 2.

**Prior on settlement.** Of the 19 cards left, the settlement value and how many cards give it are:

| Settlement | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cards | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 |

The prior mean is 71/19 ≈ 3.7.

**Estimate of alpha.** The history shows several trades or non-trades that an informed counterparty would not have made, so they came from noise traders. Examples:
- Round 2: someone bought at 4.8 when settlement was 0.
- Round 3: someone bought at 5.1 when settlement was 5.
- Round 5: someone bought at 9 when settlement was 9.

This makes alpha = 0.9 unlikely. Alpha is most likely 0.5, possibly 0.05.

**Update from this round's flow.**
- At quote 1, someone sold to me at 2.3. That points to a low settlement.
- At quote 2, nobody traded against 0.8 / 3.0. An informed counterparty would only hold back if settlement were 1 or 2.
- Taken together, the posterior concentrates on settlement values of 1 and 2, with some weight on 0.
- With alpha = 0.5, the posterior mean is about 1.7. Mixing in alpha = 0.05 raises it to roughly 2.0–2.3.

**Quote.**
- Ask 2.5: an informed buyer would only take it if settlement is 4 or more, which is now unlikely. Selling there also flattens my long position at a good price.
- Bid 0.6: an informed seller would only hit it if settlement is 0.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 2.5}

With card 1 = 14 the value is 14 − card 2, so it can be 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 or 10. Nothing between 2 and 4 is possible. The trades this round point to a fair value around 2.0.

**Reading the flow this round**
- Quote 1: they sold to me at 2.3. An informed trader would do that only if the value is 2 or less.
- Quote 2: no trade with bid 0.8 and ask 3. That rules out an informed trader with value 0.
- Quote 3: they bought from me at 2.5. An informed trader would do that only if the value is 4 or more.
- Quotes 1 and 3 contradict each other, so at least one came from a noise trader.

**Mixing over alpha**
- Earlier rounds suggest alpha is probably 0.5 or 0.9. I put rough weights of 0.5 and 0.4 on those, and 0.1 on alpha = 0.05.
- Mixing over those, the value is most likely 1 or 2. There is a small tail of 4 or more, about 5% weighted by the chance the counterparty is informed.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Ask 4.0:** Only an informed trader with a value of 5 or more would buy. Noise buyers pay about 2 above fair value, which roughly offsets losses to that small informed tail. Expected profit is about +0.01.
- **Bid 1.0:** Only an informed trader with value 0 would sell; one with value 1 would not. Noise sellers give me about 1.0 of edge. Expected profit is about +0.08. Moving the bid up to 1.5 turns it negative, because informed traders with value 1 would also sell.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.0}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 5, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Quote 3.0 bid / 8.0 ask: a wide spread, because the share of informed traders is unknown and could be high.

**Expected settlement.** Die 2 has an expected value of 3.0. Taking the larger of the two dice for each die 1 face gives:

| Die 1 | Expected settlement |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3.0 |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | 5.17 |
| 7, 8, 9 | the die 1 value itself |

Averaging over the eight die 1 faces gives a fair value of about **6.21**. The standard deviation is about 2.2.

**Adverse selection.** The informed share could be as high as 0.9, and on average it is about 0.48. Informed traders hurt us in the tails:
- **High tail:** the settlement is 8 or more with probability 25%.
- **Low tail:** it is 4 or less with probability 1/6, and those low values are far below fair value.

**Ask side.**
- At 7.5 the ask roughly breaks even when the informed share is 0.5.
- At about 8.0 the informed loss is small: they only buy when the value is 9.
- Meanwhile about 10% of noise traders still buy, earning about 1.9 each.

**Bid side.**
- A bid at 4.5 or 3.5 loses money if the informed share is 0.5, because informed traders sell when the value is 1 or 2.
- A low bid around 3.0 limits that loss.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 8.0}

No information so far, so I'm quoting around the prior expected value with a spread wide enough to cover informed traders.

**Expected value of the contract.** Die 2 is 1 with probability 1/2, and 4, 5 or 6 with probability 1/6 each. For each face of die 1, the expected maximum is:

| Die 1 | Expected max |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3 |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | about 5.17 |
| 7 (3 faces) | 7 |
| 8 | 8 |
| 9 | 9 |

Averaging over the 8 faces of die 1 gives an expected value of about 6.21.

**What the first quote told me.** Nobody traded at 3 / 8, which only slightly suggests the value is between 3 and 8. I'm treating the fair value as roughly 6.2.

**Choice of spread.** The distribution is lumpy:
- The value is exactly 7 with probability 3/8.
- It is 8 or 9 with probability 2/8.
- It is low (1 to 5) otherwise.

Because the share of informed traders is unknown, I'm keeping the spread fairly wide. The ask sits just above 7 and the bid sits below 5.

{"bid": 4.8, "ask": 7.6}

Die 1 is 7, and every face of die 2 (1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6) is 7 or lower. So the settlement is certainly 7.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 7. If my bid is below 7 and my ask is above 7, they never trade with me.
- **Noise traders:** they value it at 7 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.5. They trade only when their valuation lands outside my quotes.
- **Choosing the half-spread:** each side earns about x · P(noise > x), where x is the distance from 7. With σ = 1.5 this is largest near x ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 1.1.
- **Quote:** that gives bid 5.9 and ask 8.1, centred on 7, with no risk from adverse selection.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Die 1 is 7, and every face of die 2 (1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6) is below 7. So the contract settles at exactly 7, with no uncertainty left.

This changes who can trade against me:
- **Informed traders** value the contract at 7. They will not trade at any bid below 7 or any ask above 7, so they cannot cost me anything.
- **Noise traders** value it at 7 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.5. They are the only ones who will trade, and each trade with them is pure profit.

For a half-spread s on each side, the expected profit per side is s × P(noise > s). This peaks at about s = 0.75 × 1.5 ≈ 1.1. I'll keep the same symmetric quote of 5.9 / 8.1 around the certain value of 7.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

The contract's expected value from public information alone is about **6.21**:

| Die 1 | Expected max given die 1 |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3 (the mean of die 2) |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | 5.17 |
| 7, 8, 9 | 7, 8, 9 |

Averaging over the 8 faces of die 1 gives 49.67 / 8 ≈ 6.21.

Round 1 had no trades, so I still know little about alpha. Its prior mean is about 0.48.

- **Ask side:** At an ask near 7.5–7.6, an informed buyer only trades when the value is 8 or 9. That happens with probability 1/4, and I lose about 0.9 each time. A noise buyer trades about 18% of the time, and I gain about 1.3 each time. At the prior alpha this comes out slightly positive.
- **Bid side:** Low outcomes like 1 or 2 have probability 1/8 and are far below fair value. A bid near 4.8 loses money to informed sellers on balance, since I'd lose about 0.45 × alpha against about 0.24 × (1 − alpha) gained from noise sellers. Lowering the bid toward 3.5 cuts that adverse selection a lot. It also keeps a small chance of a trade, which would tell me something about alpha.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 7.5}

Fair value is the expected largest of the two dice, which is about 6.21.

| Die 1 | Chance | Expected largest of the two dice |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1/8 | 3.00 |
| 2 | 1/8 | 3.50 |
| 5 | 1/8 | 5.17 |
| 7 | 3/8 | 7.00 |
| 8 | 1/8 | 8.00 |
| 9 | 1/8 | 9.00 |

Averaging these gives (3 + 3.5 + 5.17 + 21 + 8 + 9) / 8 ≈ 6.21.

- **Quote width:** The settlement value is spread widely, with lows around 0–3 and 8 or 9 possible. The share of informed traders is unknown, and they would profit badly from a tight quote, so I keep the spread fairly wide around 6.2.
- **Last quote:** No trade at 3.5 / 7.5 tells me little. It slightly favours a value between those prices, such as 7.
- **Asymmetry:** I set the ask around 7.6 so I don't sell cheaply when the outcome is 8 or 9. I set the bid around 4.6, which limits losses to informed sellers when the true value is low.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 7.6}

Die 1 is 7, and every face of die 2 (1, 4, 5, 6) is below 7. So the contract settles at exactly 7, and everyone can see that.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at 7. They will not trade as long as my bid is below 7 and my ask is above 7.
- **Noise traders** value it at 7 plus noise with standard deviation 1.5.
- **Best spread:** I want the distance x from 7 that maximises x × P(noise > x). That peaks at about 0.75 standard deviations, so x is about 1.1.

That gives a bid of 5.9 and an ask of 8.1.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Die 1 = 7, and every face of die 2 is at most 6. So the contract settles at exactly 7, with no uncertainty left.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at 7. They will not trade as long as my bid is below 7 and my ask is above 7.

- **Best spread:** quoting each side about x away from 7 earns x × P(noise > x) per quote. This is largest at x ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 1.1, so the bid goes to 5.9 and the ask to 8.1.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

| Die 1 | Expected max |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3 |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | ≈5.17 |
| 7, 7, 7 | 7 each |
| 8 | 8 |
| 9 | 9 |

- About 25% are 8 or 9.
- About 17% are 4 or less.

**Evidence on trader type.** In round 2, someone bought at 8.1 when the value was 7. An informed trader would not do that, so it was a noise trade. That nudges alpha lower, but I'm still uncertain, so I'll keep the spread fairly wide.

**Quote.**
- **Bid 4.6:** informed traders would only sell here on outcomes of 4 or less (about 17%). Noise traders sell with about 13% probability, at a good edge.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 7.6}

Fair value with nothing revealed is E[max] ≈ 6.2, so I'm quoting 4.9 / 7.6 around it.

- That makes very high alpha (0.9) less likely.

**Risk from informed traders:**
- Values of 8 or 9 (probability about 1/4) would hit my ask.
- Low outcomes would hit my bid.

Alpha looks moderate-to-low, so I'll tighten the bid slightly.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 7.6}

Die 1 showed 7, and die 2's highest face is 6. So the contract settles at exactly 7, whatever die 2 is.

**Informed traders:** their valuation is 7. With a bid below 7 and an ask above 7, they will not trade.

**Noise traders:** their valuation is 7 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.5. Expected profit per side is about h·(1−Φ(h/1.5)), where h is the distance from 7 to my quote. That is largest when h is about 0.75 × 1.5, roughly 1.1.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

- If die 1 is 2, it is 3.5.
- If die 1 is 5, it is about 5.17.

Averaging over die 1 gives a fair value of about **6.21**.

**Settlement distribution.** Over 48 equally weighted cases:

| Value | 1 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cases out of 48 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 7 | 3 | 18 | 6 | 6 |

**Estimating alpha.** In rounds 1–3 the value was always 7, and an informed trader with value 7 never trades inside my quotes.
- Stage 1: no trades in 6 quotes.
- Stage 2: 2 noise-like trades in 6 quotes.

Comparing how likely this pattern is under each alpha gives roughly 24% for alpha = 0.05, 62% for 0.5 and 13% for 0.9. The expected alpha is about 0.44.

**Ask side.** At an ask of 8.0, an informed trader buys only when the value is 9, an expected loss of 0.125. A noise trader buys about 11.7% of the time at a 1.79 edge. Weighting by alpha, the net expected profit is about +0.06 per quote, which is close to the best I found for the ask.

**Bid side.** The low values 1 and 2 have enough probability that informed sellers would hurt any reasonable bid. Every bid level I checked had negative expected value, so I keep the bid very low.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.0}

Quote: bid 1.0, ask 9.0. The trade at 8 most likely came from an informed counterparty holding a 9, so I should sell only at 9 and avoid buying.

**What I believe about alpha.** In rounds 1–3 the settlement was always 7, so an informed counterparty would never have hit my quotes. The two trades in stage 2 (a buy at 8.1 and a sell at 5.9) were therefore noise. The many quotes with no trade also make a high noise share less likely. Combining these, alpha is about 0.05 with probability 0.24, 0.5 with 0.63, and 0.9 with 0.13.

**What last quote's buy at 8 tells me.**
- Before the trade, the expected value of the max was about 6.21.

- A noise trader centred on 6.21 buys above 8 with probability about 0.12.

**Ask.**

**Bid.**
- At any bid from about 2 to 6, losses to informed counterparties holding low values outweigh the gains from noise sellers. Expected profit is negative across that range.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Die 1 is 7, and die 2 is at most 6, so the contract settles at exactly 7. The fair value is certain.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at 7, so they won't trade with any quote strictly around 7. They pose no adverse-selection risk now.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is 7 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.5. Each side's expected edge is d × P(noise > d), where d is the distance from 7. That is largest at about d ≈ 0.75 × 1.5 ≈ 1.1.

Die 1 came up 7, and die 2 can be at most 6. So the contract settles at exactly 7, and everyone knows it.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Quoting 4.5 bid and 8.0 ask: the fair value is about 6.21, and these prices are where the edge from noise traders roughly balances the losses to informed traders.

**Fair value before any reveal.** The expected maximum for each value of die 1 is:

|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3 | 1/8 |
| 2 | 3.5 | 1/8 |
| 5 | 5.17 | 1/8 |
| 7 | 7 | 3/8 |

Stage-2 trades happened 2 times out of 8. That fits alpha = 0.5 or 0.05 better than 0.9, and my working estimate is about 0.35.

**Ask side, near 8.**
- An informed trader buys only when the value is above the ask.

- 9 → 9

An informed trader would not have made any of those trades, so all three were noise traders. That makes alpha = 0.9 very unlikely. - An informed trader sells at 4.5 only if the value is below 4.5. That happens with probability 1/6, and the average value in those cases is about 2.1.
- A noise trader sells at 4.5 with probability about 0.13.

**Ask at 7.0.**

- Expected profit per quote is about +0.18.

**Bid at 4.4.**

Being long 1 unit is fine; I'm not skewing the quotes for it.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 7.0}

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.6}

Die 1 came up 0, so the contract now settles at die 2: 1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6, with a prior mean of 3.

**Choosing the quotes**

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.0}

**Settlement distribution:**

| Value | 1 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/16 | 1/16 | 1/24 | 7/48 | 1/16 | 3/8 | 1/8 | 1/8 |

**Bid side.**

| 2 | 3.5 |

Averaging over die 1 gives (3 + 3.5 + 5.17 + 21 + 8 + 9) / 8 ≈ **6.21**.

**Ask.** Above 8, only a settlement of 9 hurts me.

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description: A custom deck of 19 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 3, 2 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 7, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dealt cards showing at least 8.

info.raw:
The contract settles at 10, 20 or 30 for the number of high cards, so informed traders cross my quotes only at those values.

**Pricing the contract.** 11 of the 19 cards are at least 8 (the 9s, 10s and 15s). The number of high cards among the 3 dealt has these probabilities:

| High cards | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0.058 |
| 1 | 10 | 0.318 |
| 2 | 20 | 0.454 |
| 3 | 30 | 0.170 |

The fair value is about 17.4.

**Expected profit of each side.** I average over the possible alpha values, which gives about 0.48.

- **Bid at 10.0:**
  - An informed trader sells only if the value is 0. An informed trader holding 10 does not sell, because 10 is not below my bid.
  - A noise trader sells about 9.4% of the time, and each of those trades is worth about +7.4 to me.
  - The net is slightly positive.
  - A higher bid, such as 12, is negative, because informed traders holding 10 also start selling.
- **Ask at 20.0:**
  - An informed trader holding 30 buys, costing me 10 each time.
  - Noise buyers do not make up for that loss, so the net is negative.
  - An ask below 20 is worse, because informed traders holding 20 also buy.
- **Ask at 30.0:** nothing trades on that side. I keep the ask there as a placeholder.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 30.0}

With 11 of the 19 cards worth at least 8, the fair value is 17.37. Informed counterparties know the exact outcome, so I'm quoting wide: bid 10 and ask 29.

**Settlement distribution.** The contract pays 10 for each of the 3 dealt cards worth at least 8. Those are the 9s, 10s and 15s.

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 56/969 ≈ 0.058 |
| 10 | 308/969 ≈ 0.318 |
| 20 | 440/969 ≈ 0.454 |
| 30 | 165/969 ≈ 0.170 |

**Why the quotes are wide.** I don't know alpha, so I use its average, about 0.48.
- **Ask:** with an ask anywhere from 20 to 30, informed traders buy whenever the settlement is 30. At asks between 20 and 24, that loss outweighs what I earn from noise traders. The two roughly break even around 28–29.
- **Bid:** with a bid between 10 and 20, informed traders sell whenever the settlement is 10 or less, which happens about 38% of the time. A bid around 15 loses money for that reason. A bid near 10 is slightly profitable: only a settlement of 0 hurts me, and noise sellers still trade occasionally.

Quoting wide but not absurdly so also lets me learn something about alpha from whether trades happen.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 29}

Card 1 is a 3, so it is not one of the cards worth at least 8. Of the 18 cards left, 11 are worth at least 8 (the 9s, 10s and 15s) and 7 are not.

**Settlement distribution for cards 2 and 3:**

| Settlement | Cards worth ≥8 | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 42/306 ≈ 0.137 |
| 10 | 1 | 154/306 ≈ 0.503 |
| 20 | 2 | 110/306 ≈ 0.359 |

- The fair value is about 12.2.
- The settlement can only be 0, 10 or 20, so an informed counterparty only hurts my ask when the value is 20. It only hurts my bid when the value is 0.
- The share of informed traders is unknown. Its prior average is about 0.48, and stage 1 produced no trades, so I have little evidence either way.
- Against that, quotes near the fair value lose money to informed traders.

**Checking candidate prices against noise traders (noise standard deviation 5.6, informed share about 0.48):**

- **Ask 18:** noise traders gain me about +0.45 per quote. Informed buyers cost me about −0.34, leaving about +0.11.
- **Bid 6:** noise traders gain me about +0.43 per quote. Informed sellers cost me about −0.39, leaving about +0.04.
- **Tighter quotes:** an ask of 16, for example, loses money on average at this informed share.

So I quote a bid of 6 and an ask of 18.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 18}

This is the last quote of round 1, so the contract settles right after it.

**Fair value.** Card 1 is a 3, so it does not count. The cards worth at least 8 are the 9s, 10s and 15s: 11 of the 19 cards. All 11 are still among the 18 unseen cards, and cards 2 and 3 come from those. The settlement value is 10 times the number of those two cards that count:

| Settlement | Cards 2 and 3 | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | both count | (11/18)(10/17) ≈ 0.359 |
| 10 | exactly one counts | 2(11)(7)/306 ≈ 0.503 |
| 0 | neither counts | (7/18)(6/17) ≈ 0.137 |

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.1 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 1/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are revealed, the fair value is 24:

- **Expected heads probability:** 0.2×0.1 + 0.6×0.2 + 0.2×0.8 = 0.30.
- **Fair value:** 10 × 8 × 0.30 = 24.

The settlement distribution is very skewed. About 75% of it sits at 0–30, and there is a heavy upper tail at 50–80 from the 0.8 coin. Without knowing alpha, I assumed roughly 0.5 when weighing informed against noise traders.

**Bid side:**
- At a bid of 10, an informed trader sells only when the value is 0. That happens with probability about 0.19, for a loss of about 1.9.
- A noise trader sells when its valuation is more than 14 below fair value, about 19% of the time. That earns about 14 × 0.19 ≈ 2.7.
- So a bid of 10 is about break-even or slightly positive.

**Ask side:**
- Any reasonable ask is costly. An informed buyer takes us into the 50–80 tail, and noise traders rarely reach those prices.
- At an ask of 40, the expected informed loss is about 4.8, against a noise gain of about 2.5.
- At an ask of 50, the informed loss is about 3, against a noise gain of about 1.4.
- So I'll keep the ask far out, where the informed loss is small.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 70}

The fair value is about 24 and the risk sits mostly above it, so I'm quoting a wide, asymmetric market: bid 8, ask 40.

- **Fair value:** The expected chance of heads is 0.2·0.1 + 0.6·0.2 + 0.2·0.8 = 0.30. That makes the expected settlement 10 × 8 × 0.30 = 24.
- **Last quote:** Nobody traded at 10/70. That hints slightly toward a value in the middle of the range, but it changes little.
- **Downside risk:** The value is often low. A settlement of 0 has a probability of about 19% and 10 about 28%. With a bid of 12, an informed seller would hit me whenever the value is 0 or 10. A bid of 8 is only exposed when the value is 0, and it still catches the roughly 16% of noise traders who value it below 8.
- **Upside risk:** If the 0.8 coin was picked, the value is about 60–70, with roughly 20% total chance of 5 or more heads. So the ask must stay well above fair. At 40, it still captures noise traders about one standard deviation above fair value.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 40}

With three heads in a row, the coin is very likely the P=0.8 one, so the contract is probably worth 70 or 80. I'll quote bid 60 / ask 80: an informed trader gains little at those prices, and noise traders still give me some edge.

**Which coin is it?** Prior × likelihood of three heads:
- P(heads)=0.1: 0.2 × 0.001 = 0.0002
- P(heads)=0.2: 0.6 × 0.008 = 0.0048
- P(heads)=0.8: 0.2 × 0.512 = 0.1024

After normalising, P(coin = 0.8) ≈ 0.953, P(coin = 0.2) ≈ 0.045 and P(coin = 0.1) ≈ 0.002.

**Fair value**
- Expected heads per remaining flip ≈ 0.772.
- Over the 5 remaining flips that is about 3.86 heads, so about 6.86 heads in total. Fair value is about 68.6.
- The earlier buy at 40, when fair value was 24, hints at an informed counterparty. That nudges fair value slightly higher.

**Likely settlement values** (assuming the 0.8 coin):

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 80 | ≈ 0.33 |
| 70 | ≈ 0.41 |
| 60 | ≈ 0.20 |
| 50 | ≈ 0.05 |

**Why bid 60 / ask 80**
- An informed trader never buys at 80. It sells at 60 only if the value is 50, which is rare.
- Noise traders still trade at these prices about 25–30% of the time, earning me about 10 per trade.
- The informed fraction (alpha) may be high, so these protective quotes are worth the narrower edge.

{"bid": 60, "ask": 80}

The contract will most likely settle at 60, 70 or 80, so I'm quoting just inside those levels: bid 60, ask 80.

**Which coin is it?** Three heads in a row strongly point to the 0.8 coin.
- The chance of three heads is 0.001 with the 0.1 coin, 0.008 with the 0.2 coin and 0.512 with the 0.8 coin.
- Combining those with the starting odds gives about 95.3% for the 0.8 coin, 4.5% for the 0.2 coin and 0.2% for the 0.1 coin.
- So each of the 5 remaining flips comes up heads with probability about 0.772.

**Expected settlement.** That gives about 3.86 more heads, so the fair value is about 10 × (3 + 3.86) ≈ 68.6. Settlement can only be a multiple of 10:

| Settles at | Probability |
|---|---|
| 80 | about 31% |
| 70 | about 40% |
| 60 | about 20% |
| 50 or less | about 7% |

**Choosing the quotes.** An informed trader only buys if the value is strictly above my ask and only sells if it is strictly below my bid.
- **Ask at 80:** an informed trader never buys, because the value can't exceed 80. A noise trader buys with probability about 24%, and I earn about 11.4 over fair value when that happens.
- **Bid at 60:** an informed trader only sells when the value is 50 or less, which is about 7% of the time, costing me about 10. A noise trader sells with probability about 25%, and I earn about 8.6 when that happens.

Both sides have positive expected value whatever alpha turns out to be.

A bid of 0 cannot be hit by an informed trader. It still earns a little from noise traders, because one with a valuation below 0 sells to me and the expected value is 24.

game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The quote below is wide because the settlement distribution is very spread out and informed traders may be common.

**Fair value.** The average heads probability is 0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.9 = 0.6. Over 8 flips that gives 4.8 expected heads, so fair value is 5 × 4.8 = **24**.

**Settlement distribution.** It is bimodal. With the 0.4 coin the mean is 16 with a standard deviation of about 7. With the 0.9 coin the mean is 36 with a standard deviation of about 4. Informed traders can therefore take a lot from a tight quote.

**Ask side.** I averaged over the three possible alpha values, weighting each by 1/3:
- An ask of 32 has slightly negative expected value. At alpha = 0.5, the noise-trader gain (about 0.64) is smaller than the informed-trader loss (about 0.92).
- An ask of 36 roughly breaks even at alpha = 0.5 and is positive at alpha = 0.05.

**Bid side.** A bid of 12 is roughly break-even to slightly positive at alpha = 0.5, and positive at low alpha.

I'll start wide and learn about alpha from the fills before tightening.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 36}

After someone sold to me at 12, my estimate of the fair value drops a lot, to about 12.4. Most of what follows is my own rough arithmetic.

**Before the trade.** Expected heads are 8 × (0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.9) = 4.8, so the expected value was 24.

**What a sale at 12 says.**
- An informed trader sells at 12 only if the value is below 12, meaning 2 or fewer heads. That has a chance of about 0.19, almost all of it from the 0.4 coin.
- A noise trader sells at 12 only if its noise is below −12, a chance of about 0.067.

**Updated beliefs.**
- **Informed share (alpha):** each possible value becomes more likely in proportion to how likely a sale was under it. The probabilities for 0.05, 0.5 and 0.9 become about 0.19, 0.34 and 0.47, so the average alpha is now about 0.6.
- **Who sold:** the seller was informed with probability about 0.72. If informed, the value is most likely 10 and averages about 8. If noise, my estimate stays at 24.
- **New fair value:** this blend gives about 12.4.

**Ask.** For asks around 20–28, I expect to lose more to informed buyers than I make from noise buyers. This is because a high coin is still possible in the branch where the seller was noise. Pricing the ask near 38–40 keeps the expected loss close to zero.

**Bid.** A bid near 4.9 is the best trade-off. Noise traders below it give an expected gain of about +0.52. Informed sellers, who sell only when the value is 0, cost about −0.12. The net is about +0.40, better than a bid of 3 (about +0.38) or 6 (about +0.26).

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 38}

After two revealed tails the coin is very likely the 0.4 one (posterior about 98%), and the stage-1 trades push value down further.

**Coin posterior.**
- The chance of two tails is 0.36 for the 0.4 coin and 0.01 for the 0.9 coin.
- So P(0.4 coin) = (0.6·0.36) / (0.6·0.36 + 0.4·0.01) = 0.216 / 0.22 ≈ 0.98.
- Expected heads in the 6 hidden flips is 6 × 0.409 ≈ 2.45, so the value from the flips alone is about 12.3.

**What the stage-1 trades say.**
- Both counterparties sold to me at low bids (12, then 4.9).
- A seller at 4.9 who was informed means the settlement is 0, i.e. no heads at all.
- Weighing the three possible alpha values against the 6-flip head distribution:
  - Alpha is probably 0.9 (about 67%).
  - P(settlement = 0) is about 86%.
- Fair value is roughly 1–2.

**Position.** I'm long 2 at an average cost of 8.45, which is probably a loss.

**This quote.**
- **Bid 0:** the settlement can't be below 0, so an informed trader never sells to me there. A noise trader who sells at 0 hands me a free option.
- **Ask 4:** a noise trader buying there pays well above fair value, which helps unwind my long. An informed trader only buys if the settlement is at least 5, which has about 14% posterior probability.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4}

Two tails were revealed, so the coin is very likely the 0.4 coin. That puts the public estimate at about 12.3 before looking at the trading.

The trading points strongly to a settlement value of 0, meaning no further heads:
- Counterparties sold to me at 12 and then at 4.9.
- At quote 3 nobody traded at 0/4. A noise trader centred near 12 would usually have bought at 4. An informed trader stays out only if the value is 0.

That pattern is much more likely if alpha is high and the value is 0. My estimate is about a 99% chance the value is 0.

I am long 2 units, so I want to sell. An informed trader won't buy at any ask above 0. A noise trader's valuation is centred near the public fair value (now close to 0) with spread 8. The profit from that buyer, P(valuation above ask) × ask, peaks with the ask at roughly 6. I won't bid, since I don't want to add to the long position.

{"bid": null, "ask": 6}

Pooling the round 1 evidence suggests most counterparties are informed (alpha around 0.8), so I'll quote only at prices informed traders can never profit from: a bid of 0 and an ask of 40.

**Settlement before any reveal:**
- The coin with P(heads) = 0.9 has probability 0.4. Its value has mean 36 and is concentrated at 30–40.
- The coin with P(heads) = 0.4 has probability 0.6. Its value has mean 16 and spreads across 0–40.
- The fair value is 24, but the outcome is very spread out.

**What round 1 says about alpha:**
- Counterparties sold to me at 12 and then at 4.9 when the fair value was about 24.
- A noise trader would do that only rarely (about 7% and under 1% of the time).
- The settlement was 0, which is exactly what informed sellers would have known.
- Updating on this gives roughly a 75% chance that alpha is 0.9, about 25% that it is 0.5, and almost none that it is 0.05. That puts expected alpha around 0.8.

**Choosing the quote:**
- With most flow informed, any ask inside 40 loses to informed buyers more than it earns from noise traders. For example, an ask of 38 loses about 0.34 per informed arrival to a settlement of 40 and gains only about 0.56 × 0.2 from noise.
- The settlement value can only fall between 0 and 40. An ask of 40 and a bid of 0 therefore carry no adverse-selection risk.
- They still collect a small expected edge from noise traders whose valuations land in the tails.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 40}

Quoting 0 bid and 40 ask, the widest possible: the settlement value can only be between 0 and 40, so informed traders can never profit against these prices.

**Who I am likely trading against.** Last round settled at 0, and both of my bids were hit, at 12 and then at 4.9.
- A noise trader sells at those prices only with small probability: about 6.7% at 12 and about 2% at 4.9.
- An informed trader who knew the value was 0 sells every time.
- So the share of informed traders is very likely high: about 0.75 probability that it is 0.9 and about 0.25 that it is 0.5. My expected share of informed traders is about 0.8.

**Settlement distribution.** The value is 5 times the number of heads, and it has two humps.
- The coin with 0.4 heads (60% likely) averages 3.2 heads, a value of about 16.
- The coin with 0.9 heads (40% likely) averages 7.2 heads, a value of about 36.
- The current public fair value is about 24.

**Edge check.**
- **Ask:** an informed trader buys only when the value is above my ask. At 40 that never happens, because 40 is the maximum.
- **Ask just below 40:** 8 heads has about 17% probability. The extra noise-trader profit roughly cancels the extra informed loss, so it is not worth it.
- **Bid:** with a 4.9 bid, an informed trader sells whenever the value is 0, about 1% likely. Expected loss is about −0.04; expected noise-trader gain is about +0.03, so roughly break-even or slightly negative.
- **Bid at 9.9:** clearly negative, about −0.29 + 0.11.
- **Bid at 0:** informed traders can never profit, so it is the safest choice and gives a tiny positive edge from noise traders.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 40}

With flips 1 and 2 both heads, the coin is likely the 0.9 coin, and the informed traders are probably the majority, so I'm keeping both sides of the quote wide.

**Which coin.** Two heads move the 0.9 coin from 40% likely to about 77%:
- P(0.9 coin) = 0.4·0.81 / (0.4·0.81 + 0.6·0.16) ≈ 0.77.
- Expected heads in the 6 remaining flips ≈ 4.71.
- Public fair value ≈ 5 × 6.71 ≈ 33.6.
- Settlement is 10 + 5·(heads in flips 3–8), so it can only be between 10 and 40.

**How many informed traders.** In round 1, counterparties sold to me at 12 and at 4.9, and the round settled at 0. A noise trader would rarely sell that low, but an informed one always would. Weighing that evidence, alpha = 0.9 is about 75% likely, alpha = 0.5 about 25%, and alpha = 0.05 almost ruled out.

**Ask.**
- An ask at 40 can never be bought by an informed trader, because settlement cannot exceed 40.
- Noise traders still buy there about 21% of the time, earning me about 6.4 each time.
- Asking lower, for example 37, gets picked off by informed traders when settlement is 40. That outcome has probability about 0.41, so the expected loss is well over 1 per quote.

**Bid.**
- An informed trader only sells when settlement is below my bid, which happens if the coin is the 0.4 one and few heads follow.
- At a bid of 20, the expected loss to informed traders (about 0.26) outweighs the gain from noise traders (about 0.12).
- At a bid of 15 the two roughly cancel.
- A bid of 10 is completely safe, since settlement cannot be below 10, so I quote 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 40}

Flips 1 and 2 were both heads, so the coin is now very likely the 0.9 coin. The best bid is 10 and the best ask is 40.

**Which coin it is.** The chance of two heads is 0.16 with the 0.4 coin and 0.81 with the 0.9 coin.
- 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.16 = 0.096
- 0.9 coin: 0.4 × 0.81 = 0.324
- So P(0.9 coin) ≈ 0.77 and P(0.4 coin) ≈ 0.23.

**Fair value.** Each of the 6 unrevealed flips is heads with probability 0.77 × 0.9 + 0.23 × 0.4 ≈ 0.786. That gives about 4.71 more heads, 6.71 heads in total, and a fair value of about **33.6**.

**How many counterparties are informed (alpha).** In round 1, both of my bids (12 and 4.9) were hit, and the contract then settled at 0. A noise trader would rarely sell that far below fair value. Updating on this gives P(alpha = 0.9) ≈ 0.76, P(alpha = 0.5) ≈ 0.23 and P(alpha = 0.05) ≈ 0.01. The expected alpha is about 0.8, so most counterparties likely know the settlement value.

**Possible settlement values.** The value is 10 plus 5 for each further head.

| Value | 40 | 35 | 30 | 25 | 20 | 15 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.41 | 0.28 | 0.11 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.04 | 0.01 |

**Choosing the ask.**
- At 40, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 40.
- A noise trader buys about 21% of the time, so I expect to make about +0.27.
- Moving the ask lower lets informed traders buy whenever the value is 40, which happens 41% of the time. That loses more than the extra noise trades earn.
- So the best ask is 40.

**Choosing the bid.**
- At 25 or 20, informed traders would sell to me whenever the value is below my bid. The expected loss is larger than the gain from noise sellers, so both bids lose money on average.
- At 15 the result is about break-even.
- At 10, an informed trader never sells, because the value cannot be below 10. Noise sellers that low are rare, so the expected gain is small but positive.
- So the best bid is 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 40}

Over two rounds the evidence points to mostly informed counterparties, so I'm quoting wide, just inside the values informed traders could profit against.

**Prior value.** The expected heads per flip is 0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.9 = 0.6. Over 8 flips that is 4.8 heads, so the fair value is 24. The settlement mixes the two coins:

| Value | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | 35 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | ≈1% | ≈5% | ≈12.5% | ≈17% | ≈14% | ≈9% | ≈8% | ≈16% | ≈17% |

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 39.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.1 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.6 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Pricing the coin before any flips are revealed:
- **Expected P(heads):** 0.5·0.1 + 0.1·0.5 + 0.4·0.6 = 0.34.
- **Expected heads in 7 flips:** 7 × 0.34 = 2.38.
- **Fair value:** 5 × 2.38 ≈ 11.9.

The settlement value has two clusters, depending on which coin was picked:
- **Low coin (p = 0.1):** settlement is mostly 0–10. There is about a 24% chance of 0 heads, which settles at 0.
- **High coin (p = 0.6 or 0.5):** settlement is around 20–25.

The share of informed traders is unknown and could be as high as 0.9. They would hit any tight quote hard, because their information sits in those two clusters. So I quote wide: bid 5, ask 19.
- **Informed sellers:** they only sell to me when 0 heads come up. That happens about 24% of the time and costs me about 5 each time.
- **Informed buyers:** they buy when there are 4 or more heads, about 33% of the time. That costs me about 5 or more each time.
- **Noise traders:** about 16% of them trade on each side, and I gain about 7 on each of those trades.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 19}

The prior fair value is 11.9. The buy at 19 pushes my estimate of the settlement value to about 20.

**Prior.** The expected heads probability is 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 = 0.34. Over 7 flips that is 2.38 expected heads, so the contract is worth about 11.9 before any trades.

**What the buy at 19 means.**
- An informed buyer at 19 must know the value is at least 20, which means 4 or more heads.
- A noise trader values the contract at 11.9 plus noise with standard deviation 7. It buys at 19 only about 16% of the time.
- So the buy is fairly strong evidence for the 0.5 or 0.6 coin, and for a high alpha.

**Updated estimate.** Combining the likelihoods over the three coins and the three alpha values gives an expected settlement of about 20. Noise traders' valuations are now also centred near 20.

**Quote.** The value is still bimodal: about 3.5 if the coin is 0.1, versus 17.5 to 21 if it is 0.5 or 0.6. Informed traders may also be common, so I keep a wide spread. Since I'm short 1, I skew the bid slightly up to make buying back a bit more likely.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 25}

Given flips 0, 0, 1, the coin posterior is about 0.44 for p=0.1, 0.14 for p=0.5 and 0.42 for p=0.6. That gives an expected 1.46 heads in the 4 remaining flips. Fair value is about 12.3, which I nudge up to about 13 because of the earlier buy at 19. I'm short 1, so I'll lean the quote slightly upward and keep it wide against possibly informed counterparties.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 17}

The coin and flips alone put fair value near 12.3. The trading so far says it is probably near 20.8 instead.

**Coin posterior after the flips 0, 0, 1.** P(coin 0.1) ≈ 0.44, P(coin 0.5) ≈ 0.14, P(coin 0.6) ≈ 0.42. The expected chance of heads is about 0.365. That gives about 1.46 more heads in the last 4 flips, so the value from the flips alone is about 12.3.

**What the trades say.** Three events all fit an informed trader who knows the value is 20 or 25, meaning at least 3 more heads:
- They bought at my ask of 19.
- They did not trade at my quote of 16 / 25.
- They bought at my ask of 17.

A noise trader produces all three together only about 1.4% of the time. Weighing this over the three possible values of alpha:
- P(value is 20 or 25) ≈ 0.96.
- Alpha = 0.9 is now the most likely case, at about 72%.
- Given a high value, P(value = 20) ≈ 0.74 and P(value = 25) ≈ 0.26.
- My estimate of fair value is therefore about 20.8.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Bid 19.5:** an informed trader whose value is 20 does not sell to me at this bid. I am short 2, so buying a unit reduces my risk. Noise sellers here give me positive edge.
- **Ask 24.9:** an informed buyer only takes this if the value is 25, and then I lose just 0.1. Noise buyers pay about 4 above fair value.

{"bid": 19.5, "ask": 24.9}

The game's prior fair value is 11.9 and alpha is most likely low, so I'll quote roughly ±5.5 around fair: bid 6.5, ask 17.5.

**Fair value.** The chance of heads on any one flip is 0.5·0.1 + 0.1·0.5 + 0.4·0.6 = 0.34. Over 7 flips that gives about 2.38 expected heads, so fair value is 11.9.

**Settlement is bimodal.**
- With the 0.1 coin (probability 1/2), settlement averages about 3.5.
- With the 0.5 or 0.6 coin (probability 1/2 combined), settlement averages about 17.5 to 21.

**Inferring alpha from round 1.** Settlement was 5, so three of the four quotes tell me something:
- Someone bought at 19 and someone bought at 17. An informed trader with value 5 would never do that, so both were noise traders.
- At quote 2 (16/25) nobody traded. An informed trader would have sold at 16, so that was also a noise trader.

My rough posterior on alpha is about 87% for 0.05 and 13% for 0.5. That makes the expected alpha about 0.1, so adverse selection is modest.

**Spread.** Against noise traders with standard deviation 7, the profit-maximising half-spread is about 5.25. I widen it slightly for the informed traders.

**Informed losses at 6.5 / 17.5.**
- At the bid, informed traders sell when the value is 5 or less, which happens about 45% of the time. The average value then is about 2.5, so each such trade loses about 4.
- At the ask, informed traders buy when the value is 20 or more, about 30% of the time. The average value then is about 23, so each such trade loses about 5.5.

With alpha near 0.1, these losses are acceptable.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 17.5}

Fair value is about 14.5, so I'll quote 9.5 / 19.5.

**Prior fair value.** The average chance of heads is 0.5·0.1 + 0.1·0.5 + 0.4·0.6 = 0.34. Over 7 flips at 5 per head, the prior fair value is 35 × 0.34 = 11.9.

**Estimate of alpha.** In round 1 the contract settled at 5, but counterparties bought from me at 19 and at 17. An informed trader who knew the value was 5 would not have bought at either price, so both buyers were noise traders. That makes alpha = 0.9 very unlikely. Most of the weight goes to alpha = 0.05, with some on 0.5. My effective alpha is about 0.15–0.2.

**Update from this round's buy at 17.5.**
- If informed, the buyer's value is above 17.5, which means at least 4 heads. That is very unlikely with the 0.1 coin (about 0.3%) and likely with the 0.5 coin (about 50%) and the 0.6 coin (about 71%).
- A noise trader buys at 17.5 about 21% of the time.
- The posterior over coins is roughly 0.38 for the 0.1 coin, 0.11 for the 0.5 coin and 0.51 for the 0.6 coin. That gives a fair value of about 14.0–14.5.

**Quote.** Mostly noise flow with standard deviation 7 calls for a half-spread of about 5 around 14.5. I'm short 1 unit, which is well inside the ±4 limit, so I'm not skewing the quote much.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 19.5}

Given the revealed flips (1, 1, 0), the coin is most likely the P(heads) = 0.6 one, and the fair value is about 21.

**Which coin it is, given heads, heads, tails:**

| Coin | Prior | Likelihood of HHT | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(heads) = 0.1 | 0.5 | 0.009 | ≈ 0.06 |
| P(heads) = 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.125 | ≈ 0.17 |
| P(heads) = 0.6 | 0.4 | 0.144 | ≈ 0.77 |

**Fair value:**
- The expected P(heads) for the coming flips is about 0.553.
- Four flips are still hidden, so expected heads from them is 4 × 0.553 ≈ 2.21.
- Adding the 2 heads already seen gives about 4.21 heads, so fair value ≈ 21.1.
- In stage 1 someone bought from me at 17.5. If they were informed, the total is at least 4 heads, which nudges fair value slightly up, to about 21–22.

**Quote:**
- I'm centring around 21.5 with a half-spread of about 4. Noise traders' valuations vary by about 7, so this still gets some of their trades, while giving some protection against informed traders.
- My position of −1 is small, so I'm not shifting the quotes for inventory.

{"bid": 17.5, "ask": 25.5}

Fair value is about 19.5, and I'll quote 15.1 bid / 24.9 ask, roughly symmetric around it.

**Belief about the coin.** Flips 1–3 came out 1, 1, 0. That shifts the coin probabilities to:
- P(heads) = 0.1: about 6%
- P(heads) = 0.5: about 17%
- P(heads) = 0.6: about 77%

On that basis, the expected number of heads in the 4 unrevealed flips is about 2.2. The fair value before using any trades is 5 × (2 + 2.2) ≈ 21.1.

**Informed share (alpha).** In round 1, counterparties twice bought from me at 17 and 19, and the contract then settled at 5. An informed trader would never do that, so alpha = 0.9 is very unlikely. I'm working with alpha of roughly 0.2–0.25.

**Effect of the sale at 17.5.** At quote 3 this round, someone sold to me at 17.5. That is about twice as likely if the contract settles at 15 or below. Updating for it moves fair value down to about 19.5.

**Quote placement.** The contract can only settle at 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30.
- With the ask at 24.9, an informed trader only buys when the value is 25 or 30. Noise traders still buy about 22% of the time, so the ask side earns about +0.77 per quote.
- With the bid at 15.1, an informed trader only sells when the value is 10 or 15. Noise traders still sell about 26% of the time, so the bid side earns about +0.74 per quote.

{"bid": 15.1, "ask": 24.9}

Prior mean fair value: E[p] = 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 = 0.34. Over 7 flips that gives 2.38 heads, so fair value is about 11.9.

The settlement distribution has two peaks. The 0.1 coin puts value near 0–10, and the 0.6 coin puts it near 20–25. So informed traders would cause heavy adverse selection.

From the history, several trades went against the settlement value (for example, a buy at 19 that settled at 5), so they were noise trades. That makes alpha = 0.9 unlikely, but alpha = 0.5 is still possible.

I'll keep a fairly wide quote centred slightly below fair value.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 18}

Fair value is about 14 after the buy at 18, so I'm quoting bid 8.5 and ask 19, roughly 5 either side.

- **Starting fair value.** With no flips revealed, the average heads probability is 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 = 0.34. That gives an expected settlement of 5 × 7 × 0.34 ≈ 11.9.
- **How often counterparties are informed.** Five past trades or non-trades in rounds 1–2 could not have come from someone who knew the settlement value. For example, in round 1 a counterparty bought at 17 when the contract settled at 5. That rules out a 0.9 informed share in practice. My estimate is about 85% that the informed share is 0.05 and 15% that it is 0.5, so roughly 12% overall.
- **This round's buy at 18.**
  - An informed buyer at 18 implies at least 4 heads, worth about 23.5 on average.
  - A noise trader buys above 18 only about 19% of the time.
  - Weighting the two cases moves fair value from 11.9 up to about 14.
- **Spread.** Most counterparties are probably noise traders with noise of standard deviation 7, so a spread of about 5–6 on each side works. I'm already short one unit, so I make the bid slightly more generous.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 19}

With flips 1, 1, 0 revealed, the posterior on the coin is about 6% for p=0.1, 17% for p=0.5 and 77% for p=0.6. That gives an expected p of about 0.553. The expected number of further heads in the 4 unrevealed flips is about 2.21, so total heads are about 4.21 and the fair value is about 21.1.

On alpha, several earlier trades could not have come from informed traders. In round 1 the counterparty bought at 19 and 17 when settlement was 5, and in round 2 one sold at 17.5 when settlement was 30. So alpha is probably not 0.9.

I'll quote symmetrically around 21 with a moderately wide spread to cover the remaining-flip uncertainty and possible informed flow.

{"bid": 17, "ask": 25}

Quoting bid 15.1, ask 25.1, which brackets the fair value of about 21.1 just inside the round-number settlement values of 15 and 25.

**Fair value.** I updated the coin's bias on the revealed flips 1, 1, 0:
- p=0.1: 0.5 × 0.009 = 0.0045, posterior about 0.060
- p=0.5: 0.1 × 0.125 = 0.0125, posterior about 0.168
- p=0.6: 0.4 × 0.144 = 0.0576, posterior about 0.772

That gives E[p] ≈ 0.553. The 4 unrevealed flips are expected to give about 2.21 more heads, so fair value ≈ 5 × 4.21 ≈ 21.1.

**Settlement values.** Settlement can only be 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30, with probabilities about 0.07, 0.18, 0.33, 0.31 and 0.11.

**Alpha.** The history points to a mixed alpha, probably around 0.5. Some trades fit informed traders: the sale at 19.5 when settlement was 5, and the buy at 24.9 when it was 30. Others were clearly noise.

**Quote placement.** With an ask just above 25, informed traders only buy when settlement is 30, while noise traders still buy fairly often. With a bid near 15, informed traders mainly sell when settlement is 10. Either way the expected edge from noise trades outweighs the adverse selection. Quotes closer to fair, such as a 19.9 bid or a 24.9 ask, would pick up the losses from the 15 or 25 outcomes, which is much worse.

{"bid": 15.1, "ask": 25.1}

The fair value before anything is revealed is about 11.9, so I'm quoting 6.5 / 17.5 around it.

**Fair value.** The expected chance of heads on one flip is 0.5×0.1 + 0.1×0.5 + 0.4×0.6 = 0.34. So the expected settlement is 5 × 7 × 0.34 ≈ 11.9. The value is split in two:
- If it's the 0.1 coin, the expected settlement is about 3.5.
- If it's the 0.6 coin, the expected settlement is about 21.

**Who I'm trading against.** I checked each of the 12 past quotes against what an informed trader would do.
- Seven outcomes don't fit an informed trader. Examples: buying at 19 when the settlement was 5, and selling at 8.5 when it was 25.
- That makes alpha = 0.9 very unlikely.
- My rough estimate is about 75% that alpha = 0.05, with the rest mostly on alpha = 0.5. So the counterparties are mostly noise traders.

**Spread.** Against noise with standard deviation 7, expected profit per side is the half-spread times the chance the trader crosses it. That peaks at a half-spread of about 5.3. I widen it slightly to allow for some informed flow, which gives quotes of about 6.5 / 17.5.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 17.5}

With no flips revealed yet, the prior expected settlement is about 11.9. Last quote's no-trade at 6.5 / 17.5 only nudges this slightly toward middle values, so I'll keep a similar spread around 12.

**Fair value**
- Expected chance of heads: 0.5 × 0.1 + 0.1 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.34.
- Expected heads over 7 flips: 7 × 0.34 = 2.38, so the expected settlement is 5 × 2.38 ≈ 11.9.
- The likely settlement values are split into two clusters. A 0.1 coin mostly gives 0–5, and a 0.6 coin gives around 21.

**What the last quote tells me**
- An informed trader would not have traded at 6.5 / 17.5 only if the settlement is 10 or 15.
- So the no-trade shifts weight slightly toward those middle values, but fair value stays about 12.

**How likely informed traders are**
- In rounds 1–3, the trades are a mix of ones that match the final settlement and ones that don't.
- That points to alpha (the chance a counterparty is informed) being 0.5 or 0.05 rather than 0.9.

**Quote**
- Because of that informed risk, and with noise traders' noise at standard deviation 7, I'll keep the spread fairly wide around 12.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 17}

Given three tails, the coin is very likely the 0.1 coin, and fair value for the four remaining flips is about 2.9.

**Posterior on the coin**
- Prior times the likelihood of three tails gives these weights:
  - p=0.1: 0.5 × 0.729
  - p=0.5: 0.1 × 0.125
  - p=0.6: 0.4 × 0.064
- That gives a posterior of about 0.905 / 0.031 / 0.064.

**Bid at 0**
- Settlement can't go below 0, so an informed trader never sells to me at 0.
- A noise trader sells about 34% of the time, and I gain about 2.9 per unit.
- Any bid above 0 lets informed traders sell whenever the value is 0, which is the most likely outcome (about 60% or more).

**Ask at 9.9**
- If I ask just above 5, informed traders buy whenever there are 2 or more more heads (about 12%), and the loss per trade is large.
- At 9.9, a noise trader buys about 16% of the time, and I gain about 7 per unit.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 9.9}

Bid 0, ask 9.9: the bid can't be picked off by informed traders, and the wide ask still earns from noise traders.

**Fair value.** After three tails, the posterior on the coin is:

| Coin P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood of 3 tails | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 1/2 | 0.729 | ≈ 0.905 |
| 0.5 | 1/10 | 0.125 | ≈ 0.031 |
| 0.6 | 2/5 | 0.064 | ≈ 0.064 |

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 6 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 6. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
I priced this from the prior.

**Fair value.** The coin's average heads probability is 0.2·0.2 + 0.4·0.7 + 0.4·0.9 = 0.68. So the expected number of heads is 5.44 and the fair value is 5 × 5.44 = 27.2.

**Settlement distribution.**

| Value | 40 | 35 | 30 | 25 | 20 | 15 | 10 | 5 | 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | ≈0.195 | ≈0.232 | ≈0.178 | ≈0.117 | ≈0.065 | ≈0.048 | ≈0.063 | ≈0.068 | ≈0.034 |

The spread is wide (standard deviation about 11.6), and both tails carry a lot of weight. The fraction of informed traders could be as high as 0.9 and averages about 0.48 over the prior. Tight quotes would therefore lose money to them.

**Ask side.**
- At 40, an informed trader never buys, because the most the contract can settle at is 40.
- A noise trader buys about 5.7% of the time and I gain about 12.8 when they do.
- At an average informed fraction, that is about +0.38 per quote.
- Lower asks such as 34–36 lose more to informed traders than they gain from noise traders.

**Bid side.**
- At 0, an informed trader never sells, because the contract cannot settle below 0.
- Any bid between about 5 and 20 loses more to informed traders than it earns from noise traders.
- The bid at 0 is essentially free.

Wide quotes also let me learn something about the informed fraction from which trades happen.

  - With the 0.9 coin, 7 or more heads (a value of 35 or more) is very likely.
